Article Title: One week of extreme heat in Europe linked to 16,000 excess deaths: Report
Article Text:
Temperatures exceeded 100 degrees Fahrenheit across large parts of Spain and Italy in late June

Around 16,000 more people than usual died across Europe during a week of extreme heat in late June, according to a report based on European mortality data. The sharp rise in deaths came as temperatures surged across much of the continent.According to The European Mortality Monitoring Network (EuroMOMO) report cited by New York Times, most of the excess deaths were recorded in northern Europe, particularly France, Belgium and Germany, where populations are less accustomed to prolonged extreme heat. These countries are generally less accustomed to extreme heat than southern Europe and have fewer systems in place to cope with prolonged high temperatures.Temperatures exceeded 100 degrees Fahrenheit across large parts of Spain and Italy in late June. However, the sharpest increase in deaths was recorded in north-western Europe, where temperatures were far above seasonal norms.The scale of the mortality spike stood out against the usual pattern in Europe, where excess deaths are more commonly recorded during winter because of respiratory illnesses. The NYT reported that the number of excess deaths during the June heatwave exceeded that seen in any single week of the previous winter.The episode came as Europe continued to face another round of extreme heat in August. Meanwhile, Brussels recorded its hottest day on record on August 14, reaching 35.9C, Belgium's IRM weather agency said, according to AFP. The areas home to at least 150 million people experienced temperatures above 35 degrees celsius that day.The heat has also fueled multiple wildfires. A major wildfire in western Germany that forced thousands of people to evacuate was brought under control on Saturday, although residents remained unable to return home, local authorities said.The New York Times reported that June ended as western Europe's hottest June on record. Researchers use excess deaths, the number of deaths above what would normally be expected based on historical patterns, to assess the health impact of extreme temperatures.Earlier, Reuters reported in July that the heatwave disrupted power supplies, forced school closures and broke temperature records in France, Spain and the UK. Euro MOMO does not publish country-level excess mortality figures, but said France and Belgium were the only European countries to record “very high excess” mortality in the final week of June.Belgium recorded its highest excess mortality during any heatwave since records began in 2000, according to the country's public health institute Sciensano.A previous major heatwave in 2022 was associated with just over 16,000 excess deaths in Europe in one week, according to European Mortality Monitoring Network data. The difference was that the most severe temperatures in 2022 were concentrated in southern Europe.With heatwaves becoming more frequent and intense, the latest mortality figures are raising questions about how countries can better protect populations as extreme temperatures become more common.
Article Summary: The sharp rise in deaths came as temperatures surged across much of the continent. Most of the excess deaths were recorded in northern Europe, particularly France, Belgium and Germany. These countries are generally less accustomed to extreme heat than southern Europe and have fewer systems in place to cope with prolonged high temperatures. June ended as western Europe's hottest June on record.

Article Title: Is Netanyahu headed for setback in Israel election? No Trump endorsement raises eyebrows
Article Text:
Benjamin Netanyahu has yet to be endorsed by Donald Trump

Trump stops short of endorsing Netanyahu

Israel's Shin Beit weighs providing Eisenkot with security detail

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ’s Likud is trailing former Israel Defence Forces (IDF) chief Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition Yashar party ahead of the October 27 parliamentary elections, according to a pre-election survey, raising the prospect of a setback for the veteran leader.Although neither side is projected to secure a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, Eisenkot’s Yashar is expected to win 25 seats—four more than Netanyahu’s Likud—if elections were held today, according to a poll published by The Times of Israel’s Hebrew sister site, Zman Yisrael.Overall, the poll showed little change in the projected strength of the pro- and anti-Netanyahu blocs. Netanyahu’s opponents are projected to win 58 seats, three short of a majority, while parties backing him are projected to secure 50 seats.Behind the two leading parties, the center-right B’Yachad won 13 seats in the Zman Yisrael poll, followed by the hawkish Yisrael Beytenu with 11 and the left-wing Democrats with nine. All three are part of the anti-Netanyahu bloc.They were followed by a string of pro-Netanyahu parties. The Haredi factions Shas and United Torah Judaism would each win eight seats, while the far-right Otzma Yehudit and Religious Zionism would take seven and six, respectively.In another setback for Netanyahu, US President Donald Trump stopped short of endorsing him during the Israeli premier’s July 28 visit to the White House.According to Axios, Trump described Netanyahu as his “own worst enemy” and asked about his prospects in the upcoming election, including how he was performing in opinion polls. When Netanyahu hesitated, one of his aides interjected: “Mr. President, he is winning.”An official told Axios that Netanyahu’s weak standing in pre-election polls was partly why Trump had, “so far,” refrained from endorsing him.The report also said that while Trump remains personally fond of Netanyahu, the Republican president has grown “frustrated” with some of the Israeli leader’s recent policies and decisions, particularly regarding Iran, Lebanon, and Gaza.Trump has previously and repeatedly urged Israel’s president to “fully pardon” Netanyahu or halt the corruption trial against him. Netanyahu is seeking a fourth term in office in elections scheduled for October.Meanwhile, with Eisenkot increasingly emerging as Netanyahu’s leading challenger, Shin Bet, Israel’s internal security agency, is reportedly weighing whether to provide him with an armed security detail, despite the former IDF chief not being entitled to state protection because he is not considered a “symbol of the state.”Shin Bet chief David Zini was considering the move as the election campaign intensifies and amid indications that Iran has stepped up efforts to target Israeli leaders.Alternatively, Zini could seek to arrange protection for Eisenkot through the IDF or the Knesset Guard, according to the report.In June, Eisenkot’s field director wrote to Zini saying the Yashar leader had been forced to hire private bodyguards. According to reports, those guards are unarmed.The letter warned that Eisenkot would be “particularly exposed” as the campaign gathers pace, noting that the Yashar leader regularly makes public appearances whose details are announced in advance.
Article Summary: Israel's Shin Beit weighs providing Gadi Eisenkot with an armed security detail. US President Donald Trump stopped short of endorsing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Netanyahu is seeking a fourth term in office in elections scheduled for October. Netanyahu’s opponents are projected to win 58 seats, three short of a majority, while parties backing him are expected to secure 50 seats.

Article Title: ‘Always proud’: Kim Jong Un hails North Korea-Russia ties in message to Putin
Article Text:
File photo: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un with Russian President Vladimir Putin (Picture credit: Reuters)

Putin hails ‘unprecedentedly high level’ of partnership

Pallada

North Korea's Russia ties grow as Seoul seeks dialogue

Ukraine war adds to scrutiny of Pyongyang-Moscow cooperation

North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has reaffirmed Pyongyang's close ties with Russia, telling President Vladimir Putin that he is proud of the relationship between the two countries as North Korea marked the anniversary of its liberation from Japanese colonial rule.Kim's message came in response to a congratulatory letter from Putin marking the 81st anniversary of Japan's surrender in World War II.The exchange underscored the growing strategic partnership between Pyongyang and Moscow, which has deepened significantly since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.Kim said he was “proud” of the countries' relationship and expressed confidence in its future.“I am always proud to be able to expect more excellent future of the bilateral relations by leading, together with you, the DPRK-Russia ties that has carried forward the history of common struggle,” Kim said in his letter, according to North Korean state media KCNA.He also expressed “firm belief” that Russia would prosper and protect its “territorial integrity” under Putin's leadership.Putin's message, delivered to Kim on Friday, described ties between Moscow and Pyongyang as having reached an “unprecedentedly high level of comprehensive strategic partnership”.“Our states are actively cooperating in all the sectors while making concerted efforts to ensure the regional security and stability,” Putin said, according to news agency AFP.Kim, in his reply, said the relationship had preserved the “history of common struggle for justice and precious traditions of friendship”.The two countries' ties have expanded sharply since Russia's invasion of Ukraine. North Korea has provided troops and weapons to support Moscow's war effort, making its involvement in the conflict its most significant military engagement outside the Korean peninsula since the Korean War.In return, analysts have said Pyongyang has received economic assistance and military technology from Moscow.The latest exchange also came as the Russian shiparrived at Wonsan port in North Korea on Saturday for a goodwill visit linked to the liberation anniversary. It was welcomed by North Korean provincial officials and Russian embassy staff, according to KCNA.The strengthening North Korea-Russia relationship comes as South Korean President Lee Jae Myung renewed calls for engagement with Pyongyang.In a speech on Saturday marking Korea's liberation from Japanese colonial rule, Lee called for talks aimed at establishing peaceful coexistence between the two Koreas.He said Seoul wanted safeguards to prevent conflict and urged efforts to replace the armistice that ended the 1950-53 Korean War with a formal “peace regime”.Lee also said dialogue could address ways to curb the expansion of North Korea's nuclear capabilities.North Korea has so far rejected Lee's overtures and has criticised planned US-South Korean military exercises as provocations.The two Koreas technically remain at war because the 1950-53 conflict ended with an armistice rather than a peace treaty.The contrast between Seoul's push for dialogue and Pyongyang's increasingly close military relationship with Moscow highlights the competing diplomatic and security dynamics on the Korean peninsula.The Kim-Putin exchange also comes amid continuing allegations about North Korean military support for Russia.Ukraine has accused Moscow of using North Korean ballistic missiles in attacks. AFP reported that Kyiv alleged this month that Russian forces had launched North Korean missiles in a strike that killed at least nine people and wounded dozens.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has also claimed that as many as 50,000 North Korean troops could be deployed to Russia, although Kyiv has not provided evidence or a timeframe supporting that claim.The growing military cooperation has raised concerns in Seoul and Washington about the transfer of battlefield experience and military technology between Russia and North Korea.
Article Summary: Putin hails ‘unprecedentedly high level’ of partnership with North Korea. Kim Jong Un says he is proud of the relationship between the two countries. The two countries' ties have expanded sharply since Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

Article Title: Qatar calls Iran’s claim ‘misleading’, denies capturing 3 pilots after March strike
Article Text:
Qatar denies detaining three Iranian pilots (representative image)

Qatar says it found remains of one pilot

Dispute centres on March attack on US base

Qatar on Saturday denied Iranian claims that its forces were holding three Iranian military pilots captured after their fighter jets were downed during a March operation, saying the allegations were misleading and came at a sensitive time amid efforts to ease regional tensions.Qatari foreign ministry spokesperson Majed Mohammed Al-Ansari said authorities had attempted to contact the pilots after they allegedly violated Qatari airspace but received no response.Qatar then acted under its rules of engagement to defend its territory, he said.“We categorically deny the claims that have been circulated regarding the detention of Iranian pilots, and we are surprised by these misleading statements at this specific timing,” Al-Ansari said in a post on X.Al-Ansari said Qatari search and rescue teams subsequently searched for the pilots and later coordinated with Iran to hand over the remains of one pilot who was found.“Qatari search and rescue teams, which possess global efficiency and expertise, fulfilled their duty to the fullest in searching for the pilots' remains,” he said.Qatar also said it had invited an Iranian team in April to examine the details of its search and rescue operations, but claimed Tehran had not responded to the invitation.“Additionally, an invitation was extended for a team to visit and learn about the details of the search and rescue operations last April, to which the Iranian side has not responded to date,” Al-Ansari said.The Qatari statement came after Iranian media reported that three pilots were captured alive by Qatari forces after ejecting from two Iranian Su-24 fighter jets during a mission targeting a US military facility in Qatar.According to Fars News Agency, General Mohammad Bagherzadeh, commander of the Search Committee for the Missing of the General Staff of the Armed Forces, identified the pilots as Javad Salehi, Abdol-Majid Dashtian and Emran Behrushian.He claimed they had been held by Qatari forces for six months and called for the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) to be given access to them.Iranian state news agency IRNA had also cited a senior military official making the claim that three pilots had been captured alive.The claims relate to the wider regional conflict that began on February 28, when the United States and Israel launched strikes against Iran, prompting Iranian retaliation against targets in Israel and US military facilities across the Gulf.Iranian forces targeted the US military presence at Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar, which hosts forward components of US Central Command, including its air forces and special operations forces. The facility is the largest US military base in the region.Qatar said the Iranian pilots entered its airspace during the operation and failed to respond to attempts by Qatari authorities to establish contact. Al-Ansari said Qatar subsequently took “the necessary measures” to defend its territory in accordance with international law.Iran had previously described some of the pilots involved in the incident as missing.Iran's army said last month that it had recovered the body of Iranian pilot Majid Kazemi, who was killed during an attack on Al Udeid in early March.The latest Iranian claims, therefore, mark a significant escalation in the dispute over the fate of the pilots, with Tehran alleging they survived and were captured, while Qatar says its search teams recovered the remains of one pilot.The allegations come against the backdrop of continuing diplomatic efforts to prevent another escalation in the region. Fighting that began in late February was followed by an April ceasefire and subsequent attempts to establish a framework for peace talks, although those efforts later collapsed.A lull in fighting has been in place since late July.
Article Summary: Qatar denies Iranian claims that its forces were holding three Iranian military pilots captured after their fighter jets were downed during a March operation. Qatari foreign ministry spokesperson Majed Mohammed Al-Ansari said authorities had attempted to contact the pilots after they allegedly violated Qatari airspace.

Article Title: Heavy rain, dangerous surf: Why Hurricane Lala is a historic threat to Hawaii’s Big Island
Article Text:
Tropical Storm Lala strengthened on the Big Island of Hawaii (Picture credit: AP)

Heavy rain, flooding and power outages raise concerns

Residents brace for a potentially destructive storm

Hawaii’s Big Island faced the threat of its first possible direct hurricane hit in 155 years on Saturday as Hurricane Lala strengthened into a Category 1 storm, bringing powerful winds, heavy rain and dangerous surf to the region.The National Hurricane Centre said Lala’s maximum sustained winds had reached 120 kmph.The storm’s centre was forecast to move over or very close to the southern end of the Big Island by Saturday evening, with forecasters warning of life-threatening flooding and mudslides.The Big Island, home to about 210,000 people, was under a hurricane warning, while tropical storm warnings were issued for Maui, Molokai, Lanai, Kahoolawe, Oahu, Kauai and Niihau.Rainfall was already falling heavily across parts of Hawaii as Lala approached. Hawaii Governor Josh Green said rainfall had reached about 5 cm an hour and urged residents to shelter in place.Forecasters warned that higher elevations of the Big Island could receive as much as 63.5 cm of rain, raising the risk of dangerous mudslides in the island’s mountainous terrain.The National Hurricane Centre forecast 25.4 to 51 cm of rain for the Big Island, with isolated totals potentially reaching 63.5 cm, according to Reuters.The storm also disrupted electricity supplies. More than 40,000 utility customers across Hawaii were without power, Reuters reported, citing poweroutage.com. On the Big Island alone, more than 31,000 customers were without electricity.Hawaiian Electric warned of possible extended outages, potentially lasting overnight. Fallen trees had also damaged power infrastructure along a 67.6-km stretch of transmission lines on the Hamakua Coast of the Big Island.The Hawaii Department of Transportation closed Hilo International Airport and said it would also close Ellison Onizuka Kona International Airport at Keahole. Commercial ports on Hawaii Island, Maui County and Kauai were also closed.The storm was also producing powerful winds at higher elevations. The Maunakea Weather Centre recorded gusts exceeding 100 mph, or about 161 kmph, on the Big Island’s highest peak.The threat has prompted residents to prepare for flooding, falling trees and extended power cuts.Bobby Camara, a 75-year-old lifelong Big Island resident, said he planned to “hunker down, cross my fingers, hope the lights don't go out” at a care home near Hilo. He said residents had been stocking up on fuel and other supplies.“I think stocking up is part of life over here... You learn to be self-reliant,” Camara said, as cited by news agency AP.Mike Caputo, a local fire captain who lives near Keaau, said his generator was ready and his 10,000-gallon water tank was full. He said flash flooding and fallen trees were among the biggest concerns.“It doesn't take landfall to create destruction,” National Weather Service meteorologist Vanessa Almanza said.The potential threat is particularly significant because a Category 3 hurricane struck the northeastern corner of the Big Island in 1871, according to research by a University of Hawaii atmospheric scientist. Lala’s latest forecast had it passing “very close to the southern tip of the Big Island”, Almanza said.The storm also raised concerns about wildfires in parts of Hawaii outside its immediate path. Strong, dry winds can increase fire risks, a concern heightened by the devastating 2023 Lahaina wildfire, which occurred as a hurricane passed south of Maui.Hurricane Lala’s approach comes as Hawaii continues to deal with the effects of earlier severe flooding. Officials have opened shelters and cancelled events, while ranchers have been advised to leave cattle in open pastures rather than potentially vulnerable structures.The National Hurricane Centre warned that Lala’s rainfall could produce “life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain”.
Article Summary: Tropical Storm Lala strengthens into a Category 1 storm. Big Island faces first possible direct hurricane hit in 155 years. Forecasters warn of life-threatening flooding and mudslides. More than 40,000 utility customers across Hawaii without power.

Article Title: 19th-century ships accidentally brought mice to islands 30 miles off San Francisco; they later reached densities of 1,270 per hectare and began reshaping the seabird ecosystem
Article Text:
The Farallon Islands Are Off Limits to Humans — but Not Wildlife

Huge mouse populations create indirect predation

Threat to storm-petrels and other native wildlife

Plans to remove the invasive mice

Measures to protect other wildlife

Accidentally brought to the Farallon Islands by ships in the 19th century, non-native house mice have reached extremely high numbers, with densities of up to 1,270 mice per hectare. The rodents are disrupting the fragile ecosystem of the islands, located about 30 miles off the coast of San Francisco. Research published in Ecosphere by the Ecological Society of America, along with conservation reports from Point Blue Conservation Science and the San Francisco Bay Wildlife Society, describes how invasive house mice (Mus musculus) have changed the food web on the South Farallon Islands. The Farallon Islands National Wildlife Refuge contains the largest seabird nesting colony in the contiguous United States. More than 300,000 breeding birds from 13 species live there. However, the accidental arrival of mice during the maritime trade era created a long-term environmental problem that continues to affect native wildlife.Research published in Ecosphere shows that mouse numbers rise sharply each autumn. At their peak, there can be about 1,270 mice per hectare, or roughly 500 mice per acre. This is among the highest recorded densities of house mice on an island anywhere in the world.The population explosion is largely linked to the island's non-native vegetation and seasonal food supplies. In late summer and autumn, when plant seeds become less available, mice turn to other food sources, including the endemic Farallon camel cricket (Farallonophilus steindachneri). The huge increase in mice then creates another ecological problem involving burrowing owls (Athene cunicularia). Migrating burrowing owls arrive on the islands during autumn and feed heavily on the abundant mice. But when mouse numbers suddenly fall during winter, the owls switch to other prey. One of their targets is the Ashy storm-petrel (Hydrobates homochroa), a globally vulnerable seabird that nests in rocky cracks and crevices across the islands.Point Blue Conservation Science has studied the Farallon Islands continuously since 1968 in partnership with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. Its research shows that owls can cause significant adult deaths among Ashy storm-petrels during winter. The Farallon Islands are home to about half of the world's breeding population of Ashy storm-petrels. The species is especially vulnerable because it reproduces slowly, with females laying only one egg each year. Even a small increase in adult deaths can therefore cause serious population declines over time. The mice also affect other parts of the ecosystem. They eat large quantities of native plant seeds and compete with native species, including endemic salamanders, for food. By consuming native seeds, mice can also help invasive plants such as maritime goldfields spread. This can reduce native vegetation that provides important soil protection and nesting habitat.To address the problem, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, with support from Point Blue Conservation Science and other conservation groups, developed the South Farallon Islands Invasive House Mouse Eradication Project. The plan involves spreading rodenticide bait from helicopters during late autumn. The timing is designed to coincide with the period when mouse numbers naturally begin to decline and seabird numbers on the island are at their lowest. The rodenticide planned for the project is Brodifacoum-25D Conservation. Similar rodent removal projects have been carried out on more than 700 islands around the world. In many cases, removing invasive rodents has allowed native ecosystems and seabird populations to recover. The Farallon project went through years of environmental review. In December 2021, the California Coastal Commission approved the plan, concluding that the long-term ecological benefits of removing the mice outweighed the short-term risks of the operation.Because rodenticide can also affect animals that are not the intended target, conservation teams have developed several safety measures. Gulls, birds of prey and marine mammals could be exposed to the poison either directly or by eating contaminated animals. Resident burrowing owls are therefore planned to be captured and temporarily moved to the mainland until the bait residue has broken down. Wildlife managers also plan to keep Western Gulls away from the island during bait application. Proposed methods include pyrotechnics, sound-based deterrents and trained falcons. According to Point Blue Conservation Science, removing the mice could end the cycle in which exploding mouse populations attract owls that later prey on storm-petrels. Researchers also expect mouse removal to improve the spread of native plant seeds and help native invertebrate and reptile populations recover. Field teams continue to monitor storm-petrel nesting sites and vegetation on South Farallon Island as preparations for the final eradication phase continue.
Article Summary: Non-native house mice have reached extremely high numbers, with densities of up to 1,270 mice per hectare. The rodents are disrupting the fragile ecosystem of the islands, located about 30 miles off the coast of San Francisco. Migrating burrowing owls arrive on the islands during autumn and feed heavily on the abundant mice. When mouse numbers suddenly fall during winter, the owls switch to other prey.

Article Title: After facing accusations of being DEI hire, black former Cambridge professor found dead at home
Article Text:
Former Cambridge professor Jason Arday died on Friday.

LONDON: Jason Arday, the Black former Cambridge university professor, has been found dead at his home after facing relentless public scrutiny and accusations of being a “DEI (diversity, equity and inclusion) hire”.National Education Union general secretary Daniel Kebede said that Arday had been subjected to a “public and brutal takedown that unleashed a tirade of racism by the worst elements of the British media and right-wing commentariat”.The Metropolitan police said officers were called to Arday’s Battersea address just after 3 pm on Friday where he was found unresponsive. “His death is being treated as unexpected,” police said.The 41-year-old, who became Cambridge’s youngest black professor in 2023, resigned as a professor of sociology of education at the university on Aug 5 after Cambridge announced an investigation into his appointment.Originally, he was accused of plagiarising his PhD thesis at Liverpool John Moores University. But then other aspects of his life and achievements came under scrutiny.Upon resigning, Arday said: “The relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me.”Liverpool investigated the accusations of plagiarism in Feb and concluded it was not proven.But in a Substack post on July 21, US researcher Nathan Cofnas claimed he had run Arday’s 2015 PhD dissertation through a plagiarism-detection programme and found “substantial overlap with previously published work”. Cofnas concluded Arday had been “recruited to promote the ideology of DEI”. This led to a media frenzy questioning Arday’s career, achievements and qualifications.Friend Prof Simon Baron-Cohen spoke to Arday hours before he died. “Over the last few weeks since the plagiarism allegations came to national and international news, he was being subjected on an hourly basis to ridicule and humiliation. He told me on Friday morning he couldn’t leave his home as his face and name were now so well known that he was a figure of shame. He maintains he didn’t fabricate or lie,” he told the BBC. “He wasn’t coping with the loss of his career and reputation and he felt he couldn’t go on.”Jason believed there was a racist playbook to discredit black academics in universities, he added.“The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and always wanted to see the best in everyone,” his family said in a statement.
Article Summary: Jason Arday, the Black former Cambridge university professor, has been found dead at his home. The 41-year-old, who became Cambridge’s youngest black professor in 2023, resigned as a professor of sociology of education at the university on Aug 5 after Cambridge announced an investigation into his appointment.

Article Title: Why Putin’s first Kuril Islands visit matters as Russia-Japan ties hit new low
Article Text:
File photo: Russian President Vladimir Putin watches a military exercise from the board of the Varyag missile cruiser of the Pacific Fleet near Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, on Sakhalin Island, Russia

Putin visits Iturup, inspects local industry

Why the Kuril Islands are disputed

Japan protests Putin's visit

Ukraine war deepens Russia-Japan tensions

Visit comes amid wider military tensions in the region

Ukraine battlefield developments add to regional backdrop

Poll Vote & Share your view What is the best way for countries to resolve long-standing territorial disputes? Bilateral diplomatic negotiations Binding international legal arbitration 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

No breakthrough in decades-old territorial dispute

Russian President Vladimir Putin has visited the disputed Kuril Islands for the first time, travelling to Iturup as Moscow's relations with Japan remain deeply strained over Russia's war in Ukraine.The visit, reported by Russian state media on Thursday, comes after Putin oversaw military exercises involving Russia's Pacific Fleet in the country's Far East.It also comes a day after North Korea, a close Russian ally, fired a ballistic missile towards waters off the Korean Peninsula.Putin's trip to Iturup is significant because the island is among four southern Kuril Islands that Japan claims as its own territory and calls the Northern Territories.According to Reuters, Putin visited the Yasny fish-processing plant on Iturup and was shown local fishing operations. Russian television footage showed him examining large tuna and halibut and sampling fish roe.The Russian president also interacted with residents."What lovely weather you have there, just like a resort!" Putin told a group of locals.The visit followed Putin's inspection of the Pacific Fleet's flagship missile cruiser Varyag during military exercises in Russia's Far East.Russian state news agency TASS described the Iturup trip as Putin's first personal visit to the Kuril island chain.Putin had previously visited Sakhalin but had not personally travelled to the disputed islands.The dispute dates back to the final days of World War II, when Soviet forces seized the Kuril Islands after the Soviet Union declared war on Japan in August 1945.The four islands at the centre of the dispute are Iturup, Kunashir, Shikotan and the Habomai islets. Japan refers to them as Etorofu, Kunashiri, Shikotan and the Habomai Islands and maintains that they are Japanese territory.The Soviet Union retained control of the islands after the war, and Russia has maintained a military presence there.The islands are strategically important because of their location between the Russian Far East and northern Japan. They also have rich fishing grounds and deposits of minerals, including gold and silver.Around 20,000 people currently live on the islands under Russian administration, while Japan says its former residents were displaced following the Soviet takeover. Around 17,000 Japanese residents were deported after the islands were occupied in 1945.Putin's visit has drawn a strong reaction from Tokyo.Japanese foreign minister Toshimitsu Motegi protested the visit, reiterating Japan's claim over the islands."The northern territories, including Etorofu, are Japan's inherent territory both historically and based on international law," Motegi said, according to Reuters."Japan strongly protests this visit."The territorial dispute has prevented Russia and Japan from signing a formal peace treaty formally ending their World War II conflict.There have been several attempts to resolve the dispute over the decades. In 1956, Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev suggested that two of the disputed islands could be returned to Japan as part of a peace settlement, although no final agreement followed.Negotiations resumed after the collapse of the Soviet Union, but the territorial dispute remained unresolved.The long-running dispute has become more difficult to resolve since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.Japan joined Western countries in imposing sanctions on Moscow and has strongly supported Ukraine. In response, Russia suspended peace treaty negotiations with Japan and halted several forms of economic cooperation relating to the disputed islands.Moscow has also accused Tokyo of adopting an increasingly hostile position towards Russia.Putin used his address to Pacific Fleet personnel on Wednesday to criticise Japan's sanctions and its continuing territorial claims. He said Russia had previously maintained constructive relations with Tokyo over the issue during the administration of former Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe, but claimed Japan had since changed its position.He noted that Japan's current territorial claims came despite what he described as the post-World War II territorial arrangements being reflected in international documents.Putin also recalled the 1956 Soviet-Japanese declaration, which restored diplomatic relations and opened the way towards a possible peace treaty and a settlement of the island dispute. He claimed that Tokyo later refused to abide by the declaration.Russia has increasingly strengthened its military presence and activities in its Far Eastern territories as tensions with Japan have risen.Putin's Kuril Islands trip also comes against a backdrop of increased military activity in the Asia-Pacific region.The Russian president had travelled to the Far East to oversee the final stage of large-scale Pacific Fleet exercises, which began on August 4.Putin said the exercises were necessary to maintain military readiness and protect Russia's interests and security in the Asia-Pacific region. He also accused NATO of seeking to increase its presence in the region.Putin warned of rising conflict potential in the Asia-Pacific and Arctic regions, while criticising what he described as plans to deploy new weapons systems in the region.The timing was notable because North Korea fired a ballistic missile on Wednesday, just days before major South Korea-US military exercises are scheduled to begin. Moscow and Pyongyang have significantly deepened their military partnership in recent years.Putin's visit comes as Russia's war in Ukraine continues with fighting and long-range strikes intensifying.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces had recaptured about 745 sq km of territory this year across parts of the southeastern front, including 26 settlements in the Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia regions. However, these battlefield claims have not been independently verified.Ukraine has also stepped up attacks deep inside Russian territory, including a major recent strike on Novorossiysk, a key Black Sea port and grain-export hub.The attack reportedly damaged port infrastructure and disrupted operations at major grain terminals.Russia is the world's largest wheat exporter, making Novorossiysk strategically important not only for Moscow but also for global agricultural markets.At the same time, Russia has continued missile and drone strikes against Ukrainian cities and infrastructure.For Japan, Putin's visit is likely to further complicate already strained relations with Moscow.The Kuril Islands remain one of the most enduring territorial disputes left over from World War II.While there have been periods of diplomatic engagement and economic cooperation, neither side has been able to agree on a final settlement.With Russia's war in Ukraine having pushed Moscow and Tokyo further apart, Putin's first personal visit to the disputed islands sends a strong political signal that Russia has no immediate intention of softening its position over territory it has controlled since 1945.
Article Summary: Putin visited Iturup, one of the four southern Kuril Islands that Japan claims as its own territory. The dispute dates back to the final days of World War II, when Soviet forces seized the islands after the Soviet Union declared war on Japan. The islands are strategically important because of their location between the Russian Far East and Japan.

Article Title: Zelenskyy seeks 10% of US stockpile to 'destroy all Russians’ missiles’: Report
Article Text:
Zelensky urged the US to sell Ukraine 5-10% of its Patriot interceptor stockpile to counter Russian ballistic missile attacks

Zelensky describes daily efforts to secure missiles

Uncertainty over Ukraine's Patriot production

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you support the idea of the US providing more Patriot missiles to Ukraine? Yes, absolutely No, they should focus on diplomacy 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Zelensky seeks greater US role in peace talks

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has urged the United States to sell Ukraine more Patriot interceptor missiles, saying even 5% of the US stockpile would help Kyiv survive the winter, while 10% could allow it to counter Russian ballistic missile attacks.Zelensky made the comments in an interview with CNN as Ukraine faces a sharp increase in Russian ballistic missile attacks and a severe shortage of Patriot interceptors.“This year we have two and a half times less interceptors than we had in 2025,” he said. “Russia has two times more ballistic missiles per month than they had before.”“If they can sell us 10%, we will destroy all the Russians’ ballistic missiles. I have 1%.”Zelensky said Russia's intensified attacks had placed further pressure on Ukraine's air defences, particularly around Kyiv. The United Nations has said July was the deadliest month for Ukrainian civilians since April 2022.“Each night you have attacks, and four or five times per month we have massive attacks … terrible nights. Very heroic, very resilient people really. But they (are) tired.”Zelensky said securing additional interceptors had become a daily priority, involving direct appeals to the US and negotiations with other allies.“This is what I live each day: from 1% to 5%. I have some months, and million phone calls … I try to exchange something to missiles … I do some things which I can’t even share. It doesn’t mean that it’s outside of the law. But I can’t speak about it.”He said the global supply of Patriot missiles had been strained by the US war with Iran, during which American and Gulf forces used dozens of interceptors against Iranian missile and drone attacks.The shortage has left Ukraine facing growing difficulty in defending its cities against Russian missile strikes.Zelensky also said uncertainty remained over a proposal for Ukraine to manufacture Patriot interceptor missiles under a US licence.US President Donald Trump had said during the Nato summit in Ankara that he would allow Ukraine to obtain a licence to manufacture the systems. However, Trump later expressed uncertainty about the proposal.Patriot system manufacturers have since sent officials to Kyiv to discuss potential production, but Zelensky said no agreement had yet been reached.“I hope that I will get it,” Zelensky said. “I don’t have now 5% and I don’t have such an acceptance. And this is for me is a big challenge, one of the biggest I had from the very beginning of this war.”Zelensky said he had been appealing directly to the White House through calls and messages, as well as through Ukraine's allies, to secure additional Patriot support.Zelensky also said Ukraine had presented new proposals for the US-led peace process, while calling for greater American involvement.“We need more involvement of the American side to the peace plan. I’m thankful to the team of President Trump that they want to continue. (Russian President Vladimir) Putin doesn’t want to stop this war now and (there’s) not enough pressure on him now.”He rejected the possibility of Ukraine surrendering the remaining territory in the Donbass sought by Russian President Vladimir Putin, saying security guarantees remained essential to prevent another invasion.“Russia begins to speak about this war, and they speak about territory. The key question is why he will not come again with 1 or 2 additional million soldiers after a big pause. Why he will not come again to occupy us?”Zelensky also backed Western assessments that Putin could eventually seek to escalate the conflict with Nato, including by targeting the Baltic states.“He doesn’t know how to end this war without big occupation or big victory for his society. It’s more simple to find some smaller country … for him, it will not be important if this country is in Nato or not in Nato. He wants quick victory, 100% sure that he will win, occupy or destroy or control.”
Article Summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has urged the United States to sell Ukraine more Patriot interceptor missiles. He said even 5% of the US stockpile would help Kyiv survive the winter, while 10% could allow it to counter Russian ballistic missile attacks. Zelenski said securing additional interceptors had become a daily priority.

Article Title: Indian-origin teen charged with murdering mother, brother in US after ‘kill family’ searches
Article Text:
Indian-origin teenager charged with double murder of mother, brother in Massachusetts.

A 17-year-old Indian-origin teenager has been charged with allegedly murdering his mother and younger brother at their home in Acton, Massachusetts, authorities said.The teen has been charged with two counts of murder, two counts each of assault and battery on a household or family member and assault and battery, along with charges of using a vehicle without authority and stealing a motor vehicle.The 17-year old is accused of fatally assaulting his mother, Sudha Venkatesan, 45, and his 14-year-old brother, Siddharth Aravind, inside their Martha Lane home on Tuesday before fleeing in his mother's car.Middlesex district attorney Marian Ryan and acton police chief Douglas Sturniolo said police received a call from teen's father shortly after 6.37 pm on August 11 after he was unable to contact his family. A tutor expected at the house had also been unable to reach anyone.The father had last spoken to Sudha early Tuesday morning before leaving for work, while Siddharth was last seen around noon, authorities said.Police who arrived at the house found both victims dead. Siddharth was found on the first floor and Sudha in the finished basement. Both victims were found with “obvious trauma”, but the chief medical examiner has yet to release information on the exact cause and manner of death.The type of weapon used in the killings is also still under investigation.The accused was not at the house when police arrived and was believed to have fled in his mother's vehicle. Investigators issued an alert for him as they searched for the teenager.He was found early Wednesday in the vehicle in a parking lot in Wayland, Massachusetts, after local police responded to an unrelated alarm. He was taken into custody without incident.The Middlesex county district attorney's office said investigators found that Arjun had recently displayed concerning behaviour."The subsequent investigation indicates that Arjun had recently been demonstrating concerning behaviour, including using the internet and ChatGPT to make searches for theoretical ideas or fantasies regarding killing his family,” the statement said.Arjun was expected to be arraigned in Lowell juvenile court on Wednesday. However, the juvenile court does not have jurisdiction over murder charges. He will therefore face arraignment on the murder and related assault charges in Concord district court later.
Article Summary: Indian-origin teenager charged with double murder of mother, brother in Massachusetts. The 17-year-old is accused of fatally assaulting his mother, Sudha Venkatesan, 45, and his brother, Siddharth Aravind, 14. The teen has been charged with two counts of murder, two counts each of assault and battery.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Melinda French Gates: "When something's uncomfortable, it means you're actually…" - a lesson on stepping outside your comfort zone
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Melinda French Gates

Quote of the day by Melinda French Gates

"When something's uncomfortable, it means you're actually growing, so embrace that"

Where this quote actually comes from

What the quote is actually saying

Why discomfort can genuinely be a sign of progress

Why stepping outside a comfort zone actually matters

Why failure is genuinely part of growth

Why real confidence tends to develop through experience, not before it

Why this idea applies directly to professional life

A note on Melinda French Gates

Other famous quotes by Melinda French Gates

"That is why we women have to lift each other up, not to replace men at the top of the hierarchy, but to become partners with men in ending hierarchy."

"I've never held the view that women are better than men, or that the best way to improve the world is for women to gain more power than men."

"Embrace change. Don't be afraid of it."

"I am simply not willing to accept that my granddaughters could grow up with less freedom than I did."

Why this quote continues to inspire people

Growth rarely feels comfortable while it is actually happening. Learning something new, taking on more responsibility, or simply stepping into an unfamiliar situation tends to bring real uncertainty along with it. Melinda French Gates put a name to that discomfort directly. "When something's uncomfortable, it means you're actually growing, so embrace that," she said. Rather than treating discomfort as an automatic warning sign, her point is that it often means something else entirely, that an old habit or a familiar limit is genuinely being challenged, and that the challenge itself is usually exactly where real growth actually happens. Her words encourage people to look at discomfort with greater curiosity, recognising that difficult moments can sometimes signal progress rather than failure or a reason to retreat. That practice of consciously reframing discomfort as evidence of growth, rather than a signal to retreat, reflects a deliberate mental habit French Gates has clearly cultivated over years of navigating unfamiliar and often high-pressure situations herself.French Gates said this in a Forbes interview with Marianne Schnall, published in April 2025, while discussing her memoir The Next Day, released the same year. She went further in the same conversation, describing exactly how she talks herself through discomfort in real time. "I'll literally coach myself in my head," she said. "'Okay, this is hard, but I must be growing here. It's going to be okay.' And then on the other side, you actually become far more resilient. " She added a piece of broader advice in the same interview too, "Embrace change. Don't be afraid of it... just know you've got a lot of tools inside of you." For French Gates, that mindset reflects the value of recognising difficult moments as opportunities to adapt, learn and develop greater confidence.Staying inside a comfort zone usually means staying inside the familiar, where there is less uncertainty and fewer situations that genuinely test existing ability. Growth tends to happen specifically once someone runs into something unfamiliar instead, a new responsibility that feels overwhelming, a moment of speaking up that feels intimidating, a new skill that feels frustrating at first. None of that discomfort is pleasant in the moment. It is often exactly what gradually expands what a person is actually capable of. This is why people who consistently seek out unfamiliar challenges tend to develop broader skill sets over time, while those who remain within familiar routines, however comfortable, often find their growth quietly stalling without ever fully realising it.Comfort usually comes from familiarity. When something feels uncomfortable, it often simply means someone has not fully mastered it yet, and that unfamiliarity is precisely what creates room to actually learn. A first attempt at something new is rarely smooth. Repeated effort is usually what eventually turns that uncertainty into real confidence, which is really how most skills get built in the first place.Comfort zones are not inherently a problem. They provide genuine stability and give people room to recover between challenges. The real issue starts once fear of discomfort stops someone trying anything new at all. Taking calculated steps beyond a familiar routine tends to expose people to new ideas and real opportunity, and over time, the boundaries of what actually feels comfortable start expanding on their own.Growth does not only happen through success. A mistake can reveal exactly where a real weakness sits. A difficult conversation can improve how someone communicates going forward. A rejected opportunity can push someone to prepare more thoroughly next time. Rather than treating every setback as proof of inadequacy, it can just as easily become useful information that helps someone actually improve.Confidence is not always something someone has to already possess before taking action. More often, it develops precisely because they took the action despite feeling genuinely uncertain about it. Each difficult experience becomes real evidence that a person can actually handle a challenge, and that evidence is what slowly builds resilience and self-belief over time.Career growth regularly requires people to take on responsibilities they have never handled before. A promotion might suddenly demand real leadership skill. A new job might involve completely unfamiliar systems. Avoiding those moments can feel comfortable in the short term, but it tends to limit development considerably further down the line, while embracing a reasonable challenge tends to open the door to real professional growth instead.Melinda French Gates is an American philanthropist, author and advocate who has worked extensively on global health, gender equality and women's economic empowerment. She co-founded the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, stepped away from it in 2024, and went on to lead Pivotal Ventures, an investment and incubation organisation she founded to advance social progress. Her 2019 book The Moment of Lift: How Empowering Women Changes the World explored many of these same themes at length.French Gates' words offer a genuinely simple way to rethink the moments that actually make people uncomfortable. Not every difficult experience is really a setback. Sometimes discomfort is exactly the evidence that someone is learning, adapting and becoming capable of something they genuinely could not do before. "When something's uncomfortable, it means you're actually growing, so embrace that" is really a reminder to approach unfamiliar experiences with curiosity rather than retreating from them immediately. Growth takes real patience, involves real mistakes, and often just requires the courage to stay in an uncomfortable situation long enough to actually learn something from it.
Article Summary: "When something's uncomfortable, it means you're actually growing, so embrace that" Melinda French Gates said this in a Forbes interview with Marianne Schnall, published in April 2025, while discussing her memoir The Next Day. French Gates has clearly cultivated over years of navigating unfamiliar and often high-pressure situations herself.

Article Title: Where is Bashar al-Assad? Ousted Syrian dictator sentenced to death in absentia
Article Text:
Synrian Ex-president Bashar Assad (2019 photo)

where is Bashar al-Assad now, and can Syria ever bring him back to face the punishment handed down by its court?

Assad remains in Russia after fleeing Syria

Where exactly in Moscow is Assad living?

Bashar Assad, left, and Russian President Vladimir Putin shake hands during their meeting in Moscow, Russia.

Russia has kept Assad away from public life

Why Syria sentenced Assad to death

Syria sentences absent Bashar al-Assad to death over killings and torture (Image: Reuters)

Verdict welcomed by Assad's victims

Can Syria actually bring Assad back?

From Syria's president to a secluded exile

Bashar al-Assad inherited his presidency from his father

A Syrian criminal court in Damascus has sentenced ousted president Bashar al-Assad to death in absentia after finding him guilty of killings, torture, arbitrary arrests and crimes against humanity committed during the country's nearly 14-year civil war. The verdict, delivered on Tuesday, August 11, marks the first conviction against Assad by Syria's transitional authorities since his regime collapsed in December 2024. But while the court has pronounced a death sentence, the former Syrian ruler remains far beyond the reach of the authorities who now control Damascus.Assad is currently in Russia, where he and his family were granted asylum after fleeing Syria when rebel forces captured Damascus in December 2024. His precise location inside Russia has not been publicly confirmed. However, reporting over the past year has placed the former dictator in Moscow, with sources previously indicating that his family was likely living in the heavily guarded Rublyovka area, an affluent district on the western outskirts of the Russian capital.The death sentence therefore raises a central question:The most recent credible reports continue to place Assad in Moscow.Reuters reported after Tuesday's verdict that Assad "is currently in Russia", where he and his family received asylum on humanitarian grounds. His brother Maher al-Assad, who also received a death sentence in absentia, is likewise believed to be in Russia.Assad's escape from Syria came on December 8, 2024, when rebel forces led by Ahmed al-Sharaa swept into Damascus after a lightning offensive that lasted less than two weeks. The advance brought down the Assad government and ended more than five decades of rule by the Assad family.At the time, Assad's whereabouts were initially unknown. Russia's foreign ministry said he had resigned and left Syria, while reports suggested he had travelled from the coastal region before being flown to Russia. Russian state media subsequently reported that Assad and his family had arrived in Moscow and had been granted asylum.In a statement issued after his escape, Assad disputed accounts that he had planned his departure in advance. He said he had remained in Damascus until the final hours and later moved to a Russian military base in Latakia as the security situation deteriorated."First, my departure from Syria was neither planned nor did it occur during the final hours of the battles, as some have claimed," Assad said in the statement."On the contrary, I remained in Damascus, carrying out my duties until the early hours of Sunday, December 8, 2024," he added.According to Assad's account, he travelled to the Russian Khmeimim airbase in Latakia after opposition forces entered Damascus and intended to continue overseeing military operations. He said the situation at the base then became untenable and Moscow asked its command to arrange his evacuation."With no viable means of leaving the base, Moscow requested that the base's command arrange an immediate evacuation to Russia on the evening of Sunday 8 December," the statement said.Independent reporting has also described Assad's departure as a Russian-assisted evacuation. The Guardian reported in December 2025 that Assad and his sons were taken under Russian military escort to Khmeimim before being flown out of Syria.This is where the trail becomes less certain. There is no publicly verified address for Assad in Moscow, and he has rarely, if ever, been seen publicly since arriving in Russia. A detailed Guardian investigation published in December 2025, based on sources in Russia and Syria, a family friend and leaked data, reported that the Assad family was likely living in Rublyovka, a prestigious gated area associated with Russia's political and business elite.The report described the family's life in Moscow as secluded and closely controlled. A family friend said Assad had little contact with the outside world and remained in touch with only a small number of people who had served around his presidential palace."It's a very quiet life," said the family friend. "He has very little, if any, contact with the outside world. He's only in touch with a couple of people who were in his palace, like Mansour Azzam [former Syrian minister of presidency affairs] and Yassar Ibrahim [Assad's top economic crony]."The same investigation said Assad was studying Russian and revisiting his training in ophthalmology. Before entering politics, Assad had trained as an ophthalmologist in London and had originally intended to pursue a medical career before the death of his elder brother Basil changed the succession plans of the Assad family."He’s studying Russian and brushing up on his ophthalmology again," a family friend told the Guardian. "It’s a passion of his, he obviously doesn’t need the money. Even before the war in Syria began, he used to regularly practice his ophthalmology in Damascus."However, the Rublyovka location should be treated as a reported possibility rather than a confirmed current address. What is firmly established is that Assad remains in Russia and has been kept away from public political life.Moscow's decision to shelter Assad has been one of the biggest obstacles to attempts by Syria's new authorities to bring the former president before a court.Russia granted Assad and his family asylum on humanitarian grounds after the fall of his government. Since then, reports have indicated that the Kremlin has placed restrictions on his public activities.In a November 2025 interview cited by the Guardian, Russia's ambassador to Iraq, Elbrus Kutrashev, said Assad was safe in Russia but could not engage in political or media activity."Assad may live here but cannot engage in political activities … He has no right to engage in any media or political activity. Have you heard anything from him? You haven’t, because he is not allowed to – but he is safe and alive," Kutrashev said.The restrictions have contributed to the mystery surrounding Assad's life in exile. Unlike other deposed leaders who have appeared publicly after leaving office, Assad has remained largely invisible.His children, however, have had a somewhat more visible life in Moscow. The Guardian reported that Assad's daughter Zein attended the prestigious Moscow State Institute of International Relations, known as MGIMO, and graduated in June 2025. Other family members were also seen at the ceremony, although they kept a low profile.The family has also reportedly travelled to the United Arab Emirates, a destination with which it had longstanding connections. But reports said the family initially hoped to relocate there permanently and later concluded that such a move would be difficult because of the political implications of hosting Assad.The Damascus court's verdict is the first Syrian conviction against Assad himself. The court found him guilty of offences including premeditated and intentional murder, torture, arbitrary arrest and crimes against humanity. His younger brother Maher was handed the same sentence in absentia.Maher commanded Syria's elite Fourth Armoured Division and was one of the most powerful military figures under Assad. The division was repeatedly accused by opposition activists and rights groups of involvement in crackdowns, killings and torture during the conflict.Assad's cousin Atef Najib, the former head of political security in Deraa province, was also sentenced to death. Unlike Assad and Maher, Najib was in Syrian custody and appeared in court wearing a prison uniform.Najib's role is particularly important because Deraa is widely regarded as the birthplace of the 2011 uprising against Assad. The unrest began after security forces detained and allegedly tortured teenagers who had written anti-government graffiti on a school wall.The crackdown that followed helped turn local protests into nationwide demonstrations. The government's violent response contributed to the escalation into an armed conflict that eventually drew in regional and global powers.The court also sentenced several other former military and security officials to death in absentia, including former defence minister Fahd al-Freij and former military intelligence chief in Deraa Louay al-Ali.The ruling was met with celebrations in parts of Syria, particularly in areas that suffered heavily under Assad's security forces.Crowds gathered outside the courthouse in Damascus, chanting and waving Syrian flags. In Deraa, families of people killed or detained during the early years of the uprising gathered with photographs of their relatives.For many victims, the verdict carried significance beyond the punishment itself. It was an official acknowledgement by Syria's new authorities of crimes committed during the Assad era.Noha al-Masri, a prosecutor involved in the case, lost her brother during the crackdown in Deraa in 2011."We have been waiting for 15 years to reclaim even a small part of our rights, for all those who have spilled our blood, committed crimes, violated our rights, killed, and tortured us," Masri told the BBC."Our demand is that this not be the end of the trials... In the new Syria, there will be no impunity from this day forward."Reuters reported that the trial process lasted nearly four months and was presented by Syria's new authorities as part of a wider effort to pursue transitional justice after the fall of Assad.But the verdict has also drawn criticism from human rights groups over the fairness of the proceedings. The Associated Press reported that rights organisations raised concerns about whether the trials were rushed and whether defendants received adequate legal protections. Human Rights Watch also criticised the use of the death penalty, saying accountability requires a justice system capable of guaranteeing fair trials.For now, the answer appears to be no. The death sentence has no immediate practical effect on Assad because he is outside Syrian territory and under Russian protection. Syria would need Russia to surrender him or otherwise allow him to be transferred to Syrian custody.Anwar al-Bunni, head of the Syrian Centre for Legal Studies and Research, argued that the death sentence itself could make extradition harder."There is a huge problem, which is that no one will hand over a criminal to a country that issues a death sentence. This will cut off the road to Assad, and many other criminals, being handed over to Syria," Bunni told Reuters."This is performative justice, not transitional justice," he said.Syria's new authorities have previously sought accountability for Assad and senior figures from his government. The issue has also been part of the complicated relationship between Damascus and Moscow. Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa travelled to Moscow in October 2025 for talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, with Assad's extradition among the issues surrounding the relationship.Assad also faces legal action outside Syria. France has issued an arrest warrant against him over allegations connected to the bombing of a press centre in Homs in 2012, according to Reuters.Assad inherited the presidency in 2000 after the death of his father, Hafez al-Assad, who had ruled Syria for nearly three decades. Bashar initially presented himself as a modernising leader, but his rule became increasingly associated with political repression and the security apparatus.The defining event of his presidency was the 2011 uprising. What began as protests demanding political change developed into a devastating civil war involving the Syrian government, opposition groups, extremist organisations and foreign powers. Russia intervened militarily in support of Assad in 2015, helping his forces regain territory and eventually reducing the opposition's hold over much of the country.For years, Assad appeared to have survived the war. Then, in late 2024, the balance changed with extraordinary speed.Forces led by Ahmed al-Sharaa launched an offensive from northern Syria and advanced rapidly towards Damascus. On December 8, the capital fell and the Assad government collapsed.The man who had ruled Syria for more than two decades disappeared from the country and resurfaced in Moscow.Nearly two years later, a Syrian court has sentenced him to death. Yet the most important fact remains unchanged: Bashar al-Assad is not in a Syrian prison. He is in Russia, living under the protection of the country that stood by his regime during the civil war.His exact whereabouts in Moscow remain undisclosed. Reports have pointed to the elite Rublyovka district, while other details of his life suggest a tightly controlled existence away from politics and public view.The Damascus verdict therefore closes one chapter of Assad's rule, but not the question of whether the former Syrian president will ever return to the country he ruled for 24 years.For now, the death sentence exists on paper in Damascus while Assad remains thousands of kilometres away in Russia.
Article Summary: Bashar al-Assad was sentenced to death in absentia by a Syrian court. He was found guilty of killings, torture, arbitrary arrests and crimes against humanity. Assad fled Syria when rebel forces captured Damascus in December 2024. He and his family were granted asylum in Russia, where they are believed to be living.

Article Title: Indiana floods kill at least 6 as severe storms trigger record river levels
Article Text:
Murky floodwaters swallowed streets and surrounded homes in Indiana, US

At least six people, including a 4-year-old kid, died after powerful storms and flooding swept across Indiana, state officials said on Saturday. Emergency crews used boats to rescue residents from rising waters in Indianapolis.Flooding was particularly severe along the White River in Indianapolis. Footages showed water covering streets and surrounding homes in the Ravenwood neighbourhood, where residents used kayaks and rowboats to move through flooded areas.The Indiana State Emergency Operations Center said the toll also included three women and two men. Two deaths were reported in Delaware County and one each in Jennings, Lake, Porter and LaPorte counties, Reuters reported.The state Department of Homeland Security confirmed the sixth death later on Saturday, after officials had initially reported five fatalities, ABC News reported. Authorities said the storm system began hitting Indiana on August 11.Indiana governor Mike Braun said US president Donald Trump told him the state's request for a presidential emergency declaration would be approved, paving the way for federal assistance.The Federal Emergency Management Agency said federal disaster assistance was available to Indiana.Earlier in the week, severe weather also affected Illinois, Ohio and Kentucky, with tornadoes, heavy rain and flash flooding reported across parts of the Midwest. Nearly 1 million utility customers were without power at one point on Tuesday, while some outages continued in Indiana.Indianapolis mayor Joe Hogsett said the city was experiencing its most severe flooding in more than 30 years and urged residents to evacuate. Rita Reith, a spokesperson for the Indianapolis Fire Department, said 95 people and 45 pets had been rescued by late Saturday afternoon.“This is one of those once-in-a-lifetime type floods,” Jacob Spence, director of Marion County Emergency Management, told The Associated Press. “So yeah, this is an unprecedented event and unfortunately we're setting some new records.”More than 350 evacuations were reported in Delaware County, while a senior mobile home community in Tipton County was also evacuated. Rescue operations and welfare checks were under way in Fayette County, while flash-flood warnings remained in effect for parts of central Indiana.The National Weather Service said some areas received more than 11 inches (28 cm) of rain over two days. The White River rose above 24 feet (7.32 metres) in Anderson and Noblesville, surpassing records set in 1913.Authorities were continuing rescue and welfare operations as river levels remained elevated. Emergency teams were also monitoring further flood risks across central Indiana as conditions continued to change.
Article Summary: At least six people, including a 4-year-old kid, died after powerful storms and flooding swept across Indiana, state officials said on Saturday. The Indiana State Emergency Operations Center said the toll also included three women and two men. Two deaths were reported in Delaware County and one each in Jennings, Lake, Porter and LaPorte counties.

Article Title: 19-year-old held after Virginia State University shooting leaves 5 wounded, found in dorm closet
Article Text:
At least one student among 5 people shot at Virginia State University

Police have arrested a 19-year-old in connection with an overnight shooting at Virginia State University that wounded five people on Saturday. One of the victims, a 21-year-old man, suffered critical injuries.Camron Harris of Henrico was found hiding in a dormitory closet, Chesterfield County Police said, according to AP. Harris is not a student at the university, while four of the five injured people were also non-students, authorities clarified.Police have issued eight felony warrants for Harris, including allegations of malicious wounding and firearm use during a felony, AP reported. Authorities have not disclosed a motive or said whether he has legal representation.The shooting occurred shortly after 1:30 am near the university’s Quad Annexes, where campus police and Chesterfield County officers found five people with gunshot wounds outside campus dormitories. Only one of the five victims, a 20-year-old, was a Virginia State student. The victims, aged 17 to 23, were hospitalised. A 21-year-old man sustained critical injuries, while the student was later discharged and the other victims suffered non-life-threatening injuries, authorities said.The university had initially said the shooting involved multiple suspects. However, police did not provide further information on the search for additional suspects.Virginia State University, a historically Black university in Ettrick, has about 5,700 students and was the first fully state-supported four-year college for Black Americans.The incident prompted a campus lockdown, which was later lifted after law enforcement determined there was no immediate threat to the campus community. The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and the Hanover County Sheriff’s Office were assisting investigators.“We recognise the concern this incident has caused among our students, parents, alumni, friends, and the broader VSU community,” the university said in a statement, according to AP. “The safety and well-being of our students remain our highest priority.”The shooting came as students prepared for the new academic year, with classes scheduled to resume Monday. Residence halls had opened a week earlier, and many students had completed the university’s “New Trojans Experience” for incoming students.Arthur Fridrich, a former university director of distance education who lives near the campus, described the incident as particularly difficult for the community.“To start a new year with this event is very tragic. It casts a shadow in the minds of all students, and for some it will be difficult to rid their minds of this term,” Fridrich told AP, adding, “For those that were shot, my heart bleeds. I hope that they all mend and somehow do not let this event define their lives.”
Article Summary: Camron Harris of Henrico was found hiding in a dormitory closet, police said. Harris is not a student at the university, while four of the five injured people were also non-students. Authorities have not disclosed a motive or said whether he has legal representation.

Article Title: 'Unfriendly look, but we get along great': Trump posts old photo with Kim Jong Un
Article Text:
Donald Trump shared this image of him and Kim Jong Un

US President Donald Trump on Saturday (local time) shared a throwback photograph with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, joking that despite their “unfriendly look” in the picture, the two leaders “get along GREAT. ”“Despite the unfriendly look on this particular picture, there are many where we’re smiling. Kim Jong Un and I get along GREAT!” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social.Trump's remarks came ahead of the US-South Korea “Ulchi Freedom Shield” military drills, scheduled to take place from August 17-27, which North Korea has criticised.North Korea has repeatedly criticised the US-South Korea joint exercises, calling them “provocations.”On Friday, a spokesperson for North Korea's foreign ministry alleged that growing military cooperation between the US, Japan and South Korea was developing into a “nuclear alliance.”“The US-Japan-South Korea military cooperation is turning into a nuclear alliance, and North Korea will respond to a new level of threat with a new level of deterrent,” state media quoted the spokesperson as saying.The spokesperson also claimed that the upcoming drills "differed" from exercises conducted over the past five years, saying they were aimed at enhancing the countries' ability to conduct warfare based on “new aspects of modern warfare.”“It is our consistent principle of ensuring security to respond to a new level of a threat with a new level of a deterrent,” the statement published by KCNA added.Meanwhile, North Korea conducted a suspected ballistic missile launch on August 12, marking Pyongyang's second such test in less than a week.Yonhap News Agency, citing the South Korean military, reported that North Korea fired a ballistic missile toward the East Sea. The United States, however, referred to the incident only as a “missile launch.”
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump shared a throwback photograph with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Trump joked that despite their “unfriendly look” in the picture, the two leaders “get along GREAT.” Trump's remarks came ahead of the US-South Korea “Ulchi Freedom Shield” military drills, scheduled to take place from August 17-27.

Article Title: Trump eyes millions from personal political funds for GOP amid midterm pressure: Report
Article Text:
Republicans are increasingly worried that the prolonged Iran war and high gas prices could hurt voter turnout in November.

Trump turns to MAGA base

US President Donald Trump has reportedly approved plans to deploy millions of dollars from his personal political action committee (PAC), a fundraising vehicle for his political activities, to help vulnerable Republicans in the November midterm elections, while preparing to step up his own campaign appearances as concerns mount within the GOP over retaining control of Congress.Trump's political team is still deciding how much to spend, with one person familiar with the discussions putting the first tranche at around $30 million, asquoted by CNN. The money is expected to start flowing in the coming weeks, marking a late push by the president with the midterms now about three months away.The move comes as Republican advisers privately acknowledge that keeping both the House and Senate is becoming increasingly difficult. The party faces a tough political backdrop, with the Iran war and high gas prices emerging as major concerns over their potential impact on voter turnout.“There is a path where we keep the House and the Senate,” one source told CNN. “I’m not in a place today where I’m prepared to say we’re cautiously optimistic about that.”Trump is also planning to travel at least once a week to hold rallies in battleground districts, according to an adviser.The president's team had promised a more active campaign schedule months ago, but domestic issues and the Iran war disrupted those plans.With Trump's approval ratings near new lows, his advisers see little scope for winning over large numbers of independent and swing voters. Instead, they believe the Republican strategy must focus on turning out Trump supporters who vote in presidential elections but often skip midterms.“Without a doubt, we’ve got to make sure we get some of these voters who show up for Donald Trump in presidential elections to show up for these congressionals,” one adviser said.Republicans are particularly focused on battlegrounds such as Michigan, Ohio and North Carolina, where closely fought House and Senate races could determine control of Congress.But the party's campaign is being complicated by voter concerns over affordability. Advisers have told Trump that the prolonged Iran war and its impact on fuel prices are hurting Republicans, with high gas prices becoming a visible reminder of broader economic pressures.“It’s higher prices; that’s what they’re upset about,” one adviser said.Trump has nevertheless continued to defend the Iran war and has appeared reluctant to make the midterms a central focus. “I don’t have to be supporting all the people. You know, I have a busy schedule,” he said recently. “I said to somebody, ‘I won. I’m not campaigning.’”His advisers insist he understands what is at stake. A Democratic takeover of either chamber would mean tougher congressional battles for the final two years of his presidency, including the possibility of investigations and clashes similar to those during his first term.“The next two years will be f*cking horrible if we lose both chambers. And Trump knows that,” one source said.The White House, meanwhile, said Trump remains committed to protecting Republican majorities and would campaign on his administration's record while drawing a contrast with Democrats.“President Trump is the unequivocal leader of the Republican party who is committed to maintaining Republicans’ majority in Congress,” White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales said.The Trump political operation is being led by a group of longtime allies, including James Blair, Chris LaCivita, Taylor Budowich, Timothy Saler and Tony Fabrizio, with White House chief of staff Susie Wiles also involved in the strategy.
