The team is relying heavily on voter data to identify and mobilise Trump's core supporters.The strategy also comes as Republicans seek to benefit from congressional redistricting and a recent Supreme Court ruling that loosened limits on campaign spending on individual candidates. Trump and his allies believe those changes could improve the party's ability to defend its narrow majorities.
Article Summary: Donald Trump is planning to spend millions of dollars to help vulnerable Republicans in the November midterm elections. The money is expected to start flowing in the coming weeks, marking a late push by the president with the midterms now about three months away. Republicans are increasingly worried that the prolonged Iran war and high gas prices could hurt voter turnout in November.

Article Title: America’s civil war over USS Lincoln: 'Grow a pair' vs 'bring them home'
Article Text:
According to some accounts, Iranian attacks have damaged US Navy's logistics hub in Bahrain and other Gulf hubs, forcing the Pentagon to shift supply logistics to Diego Garcia.

TOI Correspondent from Washington:

A furious war of words has broken out in the United States over the deployment of a warship in the Iran conflict: whether sailors of the USS Abraham Lincoln are displaying extraordinary endurance under tough conditions or whether complaints about nine months at sea are little more than “snowflake” whining in uniform.President Donald Trump himself gave the controversy its sharpest political edge Friday when he was asked whether the aircraft carrier had been deployed too long. “No, not nearly long enough,” Trump said, adding that the USS George Washington will soon relieve Lincoln.Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth similarly rejected accounts of a crisis aboard the Lincoln, accusing “the reckless & shameless American media of completely & intentionally misrepresenting facts.” He praised the sailors for operating in “austere conditions” with few port calls, arguing that their resilience was precisely what the Navy demanded in wartime.The official narrative is colliding with a very different account from many sailors' families. At a San Diego meeting attended by roughly 200 relatives, they are reported to have confronted Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao with complaints about food, mail, sanitation, mental-health pressures and the absence of a clear homecoming date.Families describe an increasingly grim combination of exhaustion, uncertainty and deteriorating amenities: mould and mildew in showers, broken toilets, shortages of soap and other personal-hygiene supplies, degraded food choices, disrupted mail and limited hot water.Some families have also reported sailors suffering acute mental-health crises, including attempts to jump ship. The Navy says it has not observed an increase in suicide tendency on the ship, while declining to release details because of privacy and operational-security concerns.The emotional meeting underscored the unusual nature of a dispute in which the people complaining are not sailors refusing orders, but relatives asking whether the orders remain sustainable. One sailor’s wife lashed out at the President in the media, telling him, "Have some sympathy, some empathy. Take accountability for what's going on with your military, your ships, in your war.”"You're stuck in a floating metal prison, essentially, in the middle of the water, eating prison-like food with the same people in the same bunk beds in the same small quarters for 200 days, 250 days; you start to go a little insane working 12 hours, getting four or five hours of sleep," she raged.The nuclear-powered Lincoln, carrying roughly 5,000 sailors and Marines, left San Diego on Nov 21 for what was expected to be roughly a seven-month deployment. The ship has now spent more than 260 days deployed and more than 200 consecutive days without a meaningful port call — a modern record for an American aircraft carrier. The Navy's own Optimised Fleet Response Plan is designed around a seven-month deployment, explicitly balancing operational demands against sailors' quality of life and long-term fleet sustainability. The Lincoln, at more than eight-and-a-half months at sea, has therefore substantially exceeded the nominal target, even though wartime extensions are not unprecedented.One explanation for the crisis, according to some accounts, is that Iranian missile and drone attacks have damaged the US Navy's long-established logistics hub in Bahrain and other Gulf hubs, forcing the Pentagon to shift the supply logistics to Diego Garcia in the Indian Ocean. While the 4000 km distance from Iran offers protection from missile and drone attacks, it complicates the delivery of food, spare parts and other supplies to forces operating near the Gulf.The controversy also has a larger strategic dimension. The deployment to the Gulf of George Washington, until recently operating with the US Seventh Fleet in the Philippine Sea, leaves the western Pacific without a US aircraft carrier -- an uncomfortable development for the US and its allies as China expands its naval presence around Taiwan and the South China Sea.China already possesses the world's largest navy by number of battle-force ships: more than 370, compared with 296 US battle-force ships in 2024, according to the Congressional Research Service. The US retains a major qualitative advantage in nuclear-powered aircraft carriers, global bases, logistics and combat experience, but China's numerical advantage is increasingly important in waters close to its shore, which is why the Lincoln dispute is about more than mouldy showers, meagre meals, or missing soap.
Article Summary: President Donald Trump himself gave the controversy its sharpest political edge Friday when he was asked whether the aircraft carrier had been deployed too long. At a San Diego meeting attended by roughly 200 relatives, they are reported to have confronted Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao with complaints about food, mail and sanitation.

Article Title: Trumpiana: Trumpets, trombones, Turkey trick!
Article Text:
The move in apparent defiance of a judge’s May order to remove Trump’s name from what was intended as a “living memorial” for an assassinated president is bound to face legal challenges.

Donald Trump was thrilled. The Secret Service had just squirrelled the POTUS away from Turkey in a clandestine caper straight out of a spy thriller after an assassination threat from Iran.In an elaborate ruse, the wannabe super spy boarded Air Force One when leaving Turkey after the NATO summit on July 8. Then he was shuttled to a smaller plane in an airport catering truck, effectively making the presidential plane a “decoy.”Amid an uproar from unaware journalists left aboard — with several staffers and two cabinet ministers — for being taken on a risky ride, the meme maker-in-chief did not for once toot about his capricious caper. But it did fuel a fanciful flight of AI-generated memes imagining the president squeezed into everything from a catering cart to a laundry bin.A parody account calling itself the Associated Fress posted an image of Trump poking his head out of a McDonald’s truck parked beside Air Force One. Another AI-generated meme showed the president being whisked away in a laundry cart, his head emerging from a heap of towels.Iran’s state media too seized on the caper, turning it into a running joke about presidential fear, with one meme depicting a catering truck painted in Air Force One’s colours and bearing the presidential seal.“American coward-n-chief, Donald Trump, sneaks out of Turkey aboard Food Truck One,” the caption read.Back in Washington, amid a stalemate over the war with Iran, Trump threatened to declare the strait of Hormuz as “a territory of the United States.”“After we finish defeating Iran, which is being very badly defeated, pretty soon I’ll be declaring the Hormuz strait a territory of the United States,” Trump declared grandiosely in a speech at a police academy in New York.In the season of ruses, he also declared tubas, trombones, trumpets and French horns a national security threat simply to expand his terrific tariffs on aluminium, steel and copper products.Trump was stretching the national security justification a bit too far, charged critics with Wayne Winegarden, a senior fellow in economics at the Pacific Research Institute, cited by the Washington Times, saying, “I keep thinking of the ’Music Man’ song, ’76 trombones’ are invading.”In another quirky move, after nearly a decade of loudly complaining about modern U.S. aircraft carriers’ ‘complicated’ digital systems to launch jets, Trump ordered the Pentagon to redesign one using old-fashioned steam catapults instead. “It’s very complicated, you have to be Albert Einstein to figure it out,” Trump had complained to Time magazine in 2017.His order to redesign USS Doris Miller, a Ford-class aircraft carrier, that would likely cost billions of dollars, came amid reports of an intensifying mental health crisis on board the USS Abraham Lincoln, as the carrier’s 5,000 sailors and Marines endure a record-breaking deployment.Trump, however, dismissed such concerns saying the vessel had not been at sea for too long. “Not nearly enough.” But he also confirmed that the ship would now be replaced by another aircraft carrier.In yet another ruse, the Trump-appointed Kennedy Centre board voted to partially close the iconic arts centre for up to two years for renovations and to re-add the President’s name to the building’s facade, saying “Restored and Renovated” by Trump.After an almost two-hour Zoom meeting, the board voted 20-3 to change the name of the building to “The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump” and the physical location to “President Donald J. Trump Plaza.” Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick proposed the name change, NBC reported.The move in apparent defiance of a judge’s May order to remove Trump’s name from what was intended as a “living memorial” for an assassinated president is bound to face legal challenges. Truth Social’s sale of fast access to Trump’s posts too is also raising legal and ethical questions, with a new lawsuit alleging that Truth API is unconstitutional.But that’s par for the course for the Trump White House, which has faced over 80 lawsuits challenging his second-term agenda in just over 18 months, far outpacing the 121 filed in the 2017-21 first term.Trump team then went on appeal to the largely friendly Supreme Court to allow construction of his big beautiful ballroom, arguing that it was ‘vital’ for national security and that halting construction will leave Trump ‘much less safe.’Challenging an appeals court ruling blocking the above-ground construction of the ballroom without Congressional approval, it argues that “every part” of the project is “an integrated whole geared toward remedying security deficiencies and bringing critical improvements to the White House”.Given the recent attempts on the President’s life, including a shooting at the White House correspondents’ dinner in April, stalling the “vital construction” of the ballroom will leave Trump “much less safe” and ultimately risk “future presidents’ safety,” government lawyers argued.Meanwhile, citing records reviewed by it, The Washington Post reported that Trump is set to spend at least $900 million on White House construction, far higher than previously reported.Renderings of the ballroom, according to the Post, show Trump plans to put gold-colored presidential seals on the exterior of the building — a stark departure from the original vision of the White House as a restrained “People’s House” that eschewed signs of royalty.But it’s not just the top dogs who have a day in the top court. The apex court received an unlikely emergency appeal from a dog named Bruce that a California judge found to be “vicious.”But the poor dog was euthanised by Ventura County Animal Services (VCAS) before Justice Elena Kagan, who oversees emergency applications in the Ninth Circuit, could weigh in, ABC News reported. — proving that, like humans, all dogs are not created equal!(By arrangement with The American Bazaar
Article Summary: In an elaborate ruse, the wannabe super spy boarded Air Force One when leaving Turkey after the NATO summit on July 8. Then he was shuttled to a smaller plane in an airport catering truck, effectively making the presidential plane a “decoy”

Article Title: In 1958, the US moved 25 caribou to an Alaska island as emergency food for military personnel; by 2005, their herd had grown to 2,750
Article Text:
Alaskan caribou

A Cold War food reserve

Hunting kept the herd under control

The military leaves and the population explodes

Overgrazing damages the island

Caribou begin moving to other islands

A difficult problem to manage

A lesson in unintended consequences

A herd of just 25 caribou calves released on a remote Alaskan island in 1958 to provide emergency meat for US military personnel eventually grew to 2,750 animals by 2005. The rapid growth placed heavy pressure on the fragile ecosystem of the Aleutian Islands. The story of the herd has since become an example of how introducing animals for a short-term purpose can create serious environmental problems when conditions change. The population history has been documented in wildlife management reports from the Alaska Department of Fish and Game (ADF&G), along with studies by the US Fish and Wildlife Service and the US Geological Survey (USGS). Historical records show that the original transplant was a joint project involving the US Navy, Air Force, Marines and wildlife experts. During the Cold War, military planners were concerned that remote bases could be cut off from normal supply routes. To prepare for such a situation, officials decided to create a self-sustaining source of meat on Adak Island, in the central Aleutian Islands.The caribou calves came from the Nelchina herd on mainland Alaska. In 1958, they were flown to Unalga Bight on Adak Island. Marine personnel cared for the young animals after their arrival.They bottle-fed them and provided bedding until the calves were strong enough to find food on their own. The plan had two purposes. The main goal was to create an emergency food supply for military personnel stationed at Naval Air Station Adak. The animals would also provide hunting opportunities for servicemen during their free time. The island turned out to be an unusually good environment for the caribou. Adak had no wolves or bears to hunt them. Its maritime climate was relatively mild, and the island did not have the large numbers of biting insects found in many parts of mainland Alaska. The caribou also had plenty of lichens and mosses to eat.For several decades, the population remained relatively stable. From 1958 until the early 1990s, military personnel regularly hunted the caribou. This hunting effectively took the place of the natural predation that would normally help control a herd. ADF&G records indicate that hunting kept the population at around 300 to 600 animals for more than 30 years. During this period, researchers found that the Adak caribou were doing particularly well. They grew larger, produced more calves and began reproducing at younger ages than the original herd on mainland Alaska. The system worked because the number of animals removed through hunting helped balance their high survival and reproduction rates. But that balance depended heavily on the presence of the military.Everything changed in 1994, when the US Department of Defense closed Naval Air Station Adak. The closure greatly reduced the number of people living on the island. With far fewer military personnel around, hunting dropped sharply. The caribou were suddenly facing almost no hunting and had no natural predators. Their numbers began to rise rapidly. By 2005, an aerial and ground survey by ADF&G and the US Fish and Wildlife Service counted about 2,750 caribou on Adak. Later surveys showed that the population remained high. A joint census in 2012 estimated that between 2,500 and 2,800 animals were still living on the island. The herd had gone from being a carefully managed military food reserve to a major ecological problem.The growing population placed increasing pressure on Adak's limited vegetation. Wildlife experts documented serious damage, particularly in the southern parts of the island. The caribou ate large amounts of native vegetation, including slow-growing lichens. Lichen can take many years, sometimes decades, to recover after heavy grazing. Once the vegetation was removed, the animals also damaged the soil by creating large numbers of trails. These trails contributed to erosion along coastal ridges and around lakes and other low-lying areas. The problem became more serious as the herd grew. With less food available in some areas, the caribou began looking for new places to feed. This eventually led them beyond Adak Island.Adak is separated from nearby Kagalaska Island by a relatively narrow stretch of water. As the herd expanded, some caribou managed to cross the channel. USGS researchers later found evidence that caribou had established a presence on Kagalaska. Field surveys between 2010 and 2015 recorded both caribou signs and live animals on the neighbouring island. Wildlife managers became concerned that the animals could establish a permanent breeding population there and eventually spread to other islands in the Aleutian chain. In 2015, refuge managers began targeted efforts to control the animals on Kagalaska and prevent further expansion.Controlling the Adak herd remains difficult. The island is extremely remote, lying almost 1,200 miles southwest of Anchorage. Bringing hunters or professional teams to the area can be expensive and logistically challenging. After the military base closed, hunting rules were changed to allow larger harvests. However, the number of animals removed through hunting has not always been enough to keep pace with the herd's natural growth. The island's isolation makes large-scale control operations particularly complicated. The Adak caribou story also shows how strongly an ecosystem can depend on human activity. While military hunting was taking place, the population remained within a relatively manageable range. Once that hunting stopped, the same animals rapidly multiplied because there were no wolves, bears or other major predators to control them.The caribou were introduced to Adak for a practical reason. During the Cold War, military planners wanted a reliable source of food in case supply lines to the remote base were interrupted. At first, the plan appeared to work. The herd survived, reproduced and provided both emergency food and hunting opportunities. But the conditions that allowed the herd to thrive also created the problem. The absence of natural predators, plentiful vegetation and a mild climate allowed the population to grow rapidly once human hunting declined. The resulting overgrazing damaged fragile island habitats and eventually pushed some animals towards neighbouring islands. The Adak herd is now a well-known example of the risks involved in introducing animals to isolated environments. It demonstrates that a species introduced for a specific human need can become difficult to control when the circumstances that originally kept its population in check disappear. What began as a Cold War plan to protect military food supplies ultimately became a long-term wildlife management challenge for Alaska.
Article Summary: A herd of 25 caribou calves was released on Adak Island in 1958 to provide emergency meat for US military personnel. The population grew to 2,750 animals by 2005. The rapid growth placed heavy pressure on the fragile ecosystem of the Aleutian Islands. The herd had gone from being a carefully managed military food reserve to a major ecological problem.

Article Title: In 1923, wardens began protecting a 35-acre Texas island where the state’s last reddish egrets survived; one family lived there full time in a two-room hut, and today it holds the world’s largest nest
Article Text:
Welcome to the Island Where Egrets Rule

A difficult island became a natural refuge

Birds build nests at different levels

Protecting the island is still hard work

A special plant may help the birds

Climate change creates a new threat

A century of protection

A century after wildlife wardens began protecting a small island in Texas, the 35-acre site has become the world’s largest nesting colony for Reddish Egrets. Green Island sits in the Laguna Madre, a coastal lagoon in southern Texas. In 1923, Audubon Texas signed its first sanctuary lease with the Texas General Land Office to protect the island. At the time, coastal birds were under severe pressure from hunting. Their feathers were highly valued by the fashion industry, while people also collected their eggs and hunted the birds for meat. This caused Reddish Egret numbers to fall sharply across the Gulf Coast, leaving the species close to disappearing from Texas. Today, Green Island is the centre of a much larger conservation network. Audubon Texas manages 175 coastal islands, and the Texas Gulf Coast now has the world’s largest concentration of Reddish Egrets. The islands are also home to thousands of Great Blue Herons, Great Egrets, Roseate Spoonbills and Snowy Egrets. Audubon recently highlighted the history of Green Island and the continuing work of coastal wardens in a report on a century of conservation along the Texas coast.Green Island is different from many of the other islands in the Laguna Madre. Most nearby islands were created from material removed during construction of the Gulf Intracoastal Waterway shipping channel. Green Island, however, formed naturally. Its location and difficult terrain made it an excellent refuge for birds. The island is far from the mainland and is covered with thick, thorny vegetation and large numbers of biting insects. These conditions made it difficult for people to reach and also kept many land-based predators away. Early conservationists recognised that the island could provide a final safe place for Reddish Egrets in Texas. During the first decades of protection, coastal wardens lived on Green Island to provide constant protection. Some lived in a basic two-room wooden hut. Alexis Baldera, coastal programme senior manager for Audubon Texas, said the warden programme played an important role in protecting nesting birds. “Green Island was one of the first pieces of land that Audubon Texas leased from the Texas General Land Office,” Baldera said. Birds had been heavily hunted for their feathers, eggs and meat, she explained. The Coastal Warden programme created a permanent human presence to protect nesting colonies along the coast.Green Island's thick vegetation provides nesting space for many different species. The birds effectively divide the island's bushes into different levels according to their size. Large birds such as Great Blue Herons and Great Egrets usually build their nests at the top of the vegetation, where the branches are highest. Reddish Egrets, Roseate Spoonbills and Black-crowned Night-Herons tend to nest lower down, in the thick middle section of the bushes. The smallest birds, including Snowy Egrets, use the deepest branches and lower parts of the vegetation. Other species also use the island. Glossy Ibis nest on the sandy areas, while Clapper Rails live around coastal mangrove roots. A pair of Crested Caracaras also nests there. The caracaras sometimes eat young herons, but Audubon wardens do not interfere with their nest because the birds are protected.Green Island's remote location offers protection, but it also makes conservation work difficult. Audubon Texas coastal warden Brian Beller has to clear and rebuild the island's only walking trail every spring. He also removes fallen vegetation, checks for invasive predators and repairs structures damaged by storms. Although the surrounding water keeps most land predators away, some animals are able to swim to the island. Coyotes, bobcats and raccoons have occasionally crossed the lagoon. Wardens regularly check the island and remove these animals before they can reach the nesting colonies.Scientists and conservation workers have also noticed an important difference between Green Island and many artificial islands in the area. Green Island has large amounts of granjeno, also known as spiny hackberry. The shrub has sharp branches and produces small orange berries. Many artificial dredge spoil islands are mainly covered with mesquite and cactus, but they have little or no granjeno. Beller believes the birds prefer nesting in the granjeno. “That plant with the orange berries that you’re talking about, that’s granjeno,” Beller said. “Almost all of the [dredge spoil] islands out here have mesquite or cactus, but they don’t have granjeno. And that seems to be the preferred plant for the birds.” Audubon is now trying to use what has been learned from Green Island to improve other islands. Beller has started collecting granjeno seeds and planting them on other islands managed by Audubon in the Laguna Madre. The aim is to create better nesting habitat and increase the number of plants that birds prefer.The biggest threat to Green Island today is no longer hunting. Instead, rising sea levels and extreme weather are putting pressure on the sanctuary. Storms have already damaged important structures. Hurricane Hanna destroyed an elevated observation blind that wardens and visiting scientists used to count birds and study nesting colonies without getting too close to the nests. The observation tower has since been rebuilt. However, the longer-term threat could be much greater. According to computer modelling cited by Audubon, rising sea levels could eventually cover as much as 15 acres of Green Island. That would mean losing almost half of the island's current 35-acre area. Conservationists are therefore looking at ways to protect bird habitat beyond Green Island. These plans include managing vegetation on existing islands and improving artificial dredge spoil islands so they can support more nesting birds. Regular surveys will continue during every breeding season to measure nesting success and track changes in bird populations. Beller is also considering plans to restore the island's old warden hut, built in the 1950s. The building could eventually provide a base for researchers and field biologists working on the island.Green Island's story shows how long-term conservation can change the future of a species. A century ago, Reddish Egrets in Texas were being pushed towards local extinction by hunting and egg collection. Protecting a small, isolated island gave the birds a place where they could breed without the same pressure from people and predators. Today, the island supports one of the most important Reddish Egret colonies in the world and forms part of a wider network of protected coastal habitat. The challenges have changed, however. Hunting is no longer the main danger. Rising seas, stronger storms, habitat loss and changes to coastal vegetation now threaten the sanctuary. Audubon Texas is responding by protecting existing habitat, improving other islands and studying the conditions that make Green Island so successful. The goal is to ensure that the sanctuary remains a safe place for Reddish Egrets and other coastal birds for many more years, even as the Texas coastline continues to change.
Article Summary: Green Island sits in the Laguna Madre, a coastal lagoon in southern Texas. In 1923, Audubon Texas signed its first sanctuary lease with the Texas General Land Office to protect the island. The islands are also home to thousands of Great Blue Herons, Great Egrets, Roseate Spoonbills and Snowy Egrets.

Article Title: Virginia State University shooting leaves 5 injured, 1 critical; campus lockdown lifted
Article Text:
The university said that, based on the information available, the injuries suffered by the victims did not appear to be life-threatening.

(This is a developing story)

At least five people were injured in a shooting at Virginia State University in the US state of Virginia early Saturday, leaving one of the victims in critical condition.The shooting happened near the university’s Quad Annexes, which are student residence buildings, and the campus was placed under lockdown before the restrictions were later lifted.According to the Virginia State University Police Department, the shooting took place in the area of the Quad Annexes, located near the university’s residence halls. Officers responded to the 3300 block of Boisseau Street at about 1.28am.In a post on X, Virginia State University announced that the lockdown had ended but said police would remain on campus while the investigation continues.The university said, “The lockdown at Virginia State University has been lifted. A significant law enforcement presence remains on campus as the investigation into this morning’s shooting continues.”The university also described what officers found after reaching the scene.It said, “Officers responded to the 33000 block of Boisseau Street at approximately 1:28 AM and discovered five individuals suffering from gunshot wounds outside VSU residence halls.”All five injured people were taken to nearby hospitals.The university said, “All five were transported to area hospitals. One individual is currently in critical condition. The remaining four sustained non-life-threatening injuries.”Chesterfield County Police are leading the investigation into the shooting. Virginia State University said the investigation is being carried out with assistance from VSU Police, the ATF, and the Hanover County Sheriff’s Office.The university has urged anyone with information about the shooting to contact the police. The investigation is ongoing.
Article Summary: Five people were injured in a shooting at Virginia State University in the US state of Virginia early Saturday. The shooting happened near the university’s Quad Annexes, which are student residence buildings. The university said that, based on the information available, the injuries suffered by the victims did not appear to be life-threatening.

Article Title: Doom! Board lowers the boom on Indian-American CEO who fired 900 employees over Zoom
Article Text:
Vishal Garg made headlines in 2021 after he fired 900 employees over a video call.

TOI Correspondent from Washington

: Indian-American entrepreneur Vishal Garg, who became a global symbol of ruthless corporate layoffs after firing 900 employees in a three-minute Zoom call just before Christmas in 2021, has himself been ousted as chief executive of Better Home & Finance.Garg's removal came in early August when Daniel Lewis, a hedge-fund manager who had joined Better's board only a week earlier, became interim CEO. Better's board said directors other than Garg had unanimously voted to terminate him, citing concerns about his “judgment, temperament and credibility.” The company also pointed to losses exceeding $1.5 billion since 2022 and a more than 90% decline in its stock price during his leadership.The ouster is the latest twist in the extraordinary corporate saga of Garg, who founded Better after becoming frustrated with the traditional mortgage process. Born in India and raised in New York, Garg graduated from Stuyvesant High School and New York University's Stern School of Business. He previously co-founded online student lender MyRichUncle and founded Better in 2014.But it was his treatment of employees that made him internationally notorious.In December 2021, Garg abruptly told more than 900 workers on a Zoom call that they were being laid off, saying their employment was terminated “effective immediately.” He subsequently took a leave of absence amid the uproar before returning as CEO.Five years later, Garg acknowledges that episode badly damaged Better's reputation. Yet he insists that he was removed just as the company was approaching a turnaround. “We’re winning. We’ve tripled loan volume. We’re close to profitability,” he asserted in a CNN interview, describing Better as being at the “5-yard line” after rebuilding the business. He also said he felt “hoodwinked” by Lewis, complaining, “He said he liked the company’s strategy. He praised us on X and used that to get on our board and win our confidences.”The company, once valued at about $8 billion during the pandemic refinancing boom, now has a market value of roughly $300 million. Annual sales plunged from $1.5 billion in 2021 to $70 million in 2023, although Garg says 2026 revenue is on track to reach $200 million. Better has increasingly bet on AI to automate mortgage processing and has expanded into home-equity lending.Garg is not accepting his dismissal quietly, hiring a prominent law firm to regain the CEO position, and offering to work for $1 a year until Better returns to profitability. He says he has backing from shareholders holding shares with special voting powers.“It’s an acknowledgment that I’ve been doing this for 10 years, but execution hasn’t been perfect,” he conceded to CNN, adding, “I hope it gets resolved. I think the future still remains very bright for Better.”
Article Summary: Indian-American entrepreneur Vishal Garg ousted as CEO of Better Home & Finance. Garg made headlines in 2021 after he fired 900 employees over a video call. Garg insists he was removed just as the company was approaching a turnaround. He is not accepting his dismissal quietly, hiring a prominent law firm to regain the CEO position.

Article Title: US used dioxin-laden oil for dust control in a town with 2,000 residents, years later it spent $33.1 million for their relocation in order to protect their lives
Article Text:
Image credits: EPA

Signs of damage

A permanent relocation

An incineration built on the former town

Then a town, now a park

At times, things go wrong even when you try with all your might to ensure they are right. It was in the 1970s, that Times Beach, a small town in Missouri, attempted to solve a common problem for dirt roads by spreading residual oil to reduce dust. Years later, it was discovered that some of that material contained dioxin, a highly toxic substance that would trigger the permanent relocation of the Times Beach population. The situation escalated further after a severe flood of the Meramec River in December 1982. With the town flooded and contamination already identified, federal authorities advised residents not to return.Oil used to remove dustTimes Beach was located in St. Louis County, approximately 20 miles — about 32 kilometres, southwest of St. Louis. Its unpaved streets were treated with residual oil as a way to control dust raised by traffic. According to historical information published by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the oil haulier Russell Bliss was hired in the early 1970s to remove waste from a chemical plant in Verona, also in Missouri.Some of this waste contained 2,3,7,8-tetrachlorodibenzo-p-dioxin, known as TCDD, a form of dioxin.Bliss mixed the material with the waste oil that was ultimately applied to control dust. The EPA notes that the contaminated mixture was spread across more than 25 locations in Missouri, including dirt roads, horse trails, and Times Beach. The agency classifies the dioxin involved in the incident as highly toxic and associates exposure with various health damages.The first severe signs appeared far from Times Beach. In 1971, over 40 horses died at Shenandoah Stables, one of the properties where Bliss had spread the material. Birds, dogs, and cats were also found dead, and a six-year-old girl became seriously ill. Subsequent investigations linked these incidents to dioxin.In March 1982, the EPA received records from the then Centres for Disease Control (CDC), related to dioxin contamination in Missouri and began to develop plans for analysing various locations in the state.In November of that year, Times Beach was alerted to the possibility that its streets might also be contaminated. The EPA started collecting and analysing soil samples.It was precisely at this moment that a natural emergency made the situation even more severe. In December 1982, a record flood struck the Meramec River. Times Beach was inundated, and its residents had to leave their homes. The contamination was not caused by the flooding: oil containing dioxin had already been applied on the streets years earlier. Authorities feared that the water could further spread the contaminated material throughout the municipality.Given this risk, the EPA and CDC recommended that Times Beach not be inhabited again.The situation took a definitive turn on February 22, 1983. On that day, the EPA, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), and the state of Missouri announced resources for the permanent relocation of Times Beach residents.The official EPA statement released in February 1983 stated that the decision came after the CDC analysed extensive soil samples and concluded that the contamination posed a continuing threat to the health of residents.Approximately 255 samples collected after the flood were analysed. In streets, shoulders, and ditches, the concentrations found varied from non-detectable levels to 100 parts per billion. Some backyards and one residence exhibited concentrations greater than 1 part per billion and less than 5 parts per billion.The then EPA Administrator, Anne M. Burford, announced the transfer of US$ 33.1 million from the Superfund to FEMA to fund the relocation. The state of Missouri would participate in implementation and bear 10% of the costs, according to the rules established for the operation.The EPA’s retrospective indicated that Times Beach had more than 2,000 residents and that the plan involved the purchase of about 800 residential properties and 30 commercial establishments.However, removing the residents did not solve the contamination. In 1988, the EPA approved a temporary incinerator in Times Beach to treat contaminated materials from both the former town and other locations in eastern Missouri.Two years later, in 1990, an agreement established responsibilities for decontamination. Contaminated soil from other sites would be excavated and transported to Times Beach, while remnants of the former city, including structures and debris, would also be part of the cleanup process. Full-scale operation of the incinerator began in March 1996 and continued until June 1997.The numbers recorded by the EPA show the scale of the operation. In total, 265,354 tons of dioxin-contaminated materials from 27 sites in eastern Missouri were treated. Of this total, 37,234 tons came from Times Beach itself. Therefore, the more than 265,000 tons often associated with the case were not originally concentrated only within the city. The remainder was transported from other contaminated points in the region for treatment at the incinerator installed there.The historical report from the EPA on the removal of Times Beach from the Superfund priority list also states that the solid waste resulting from incineration was deposited on-site after tests confirmed that the required treatment levels had been achieved.After the completion of decontamination, Times Beach underwent a radical transformation. Houses and other structures were demolished, residents and businesses were relocated, and the land underwent restoration efforts.In September 1999, Missouri announced the opening of Route 66 State Park, located precisely in the area previously occupied by Times Beach. The EPA reported that the park occupies 409 acres, about 1.65 square kilometres, and was named after the historic Route 66 that runs through the region.On September 25, 2001, Times Beach was officially removed from the National Priorities List, the federal list of priority sites under the Superfund program. The EPA and the state of Missouri concluded that the site no longer posed a significant threat to public health or the environment and that no further remediation measures were necessary.Today, the space preserves remnants of Times Beach and also serves as a reminder of one of the most significant environmental episodes ever faced in America.
Article Summary: In the 1970s, Times Beach, a small town in Missouri, attempted to solve a common problem for dirt roads by spreading residual oil to reduce dust. Years later, it was discovered that some of that material contained dioxin, a highly toxic substance. The situation escalated further after a severe flood of the Meramec River in December 1982. With the town flooded and contamination already identified, federal authorities advised residents not to return.

Article Title: 266 days deployed: USS Abraham Lincoln to return home amid rising scrutiny over sailor welfare
Article Text:
USS Abraham Lincoln has been at centre of controversy over its prolonged deployment affecting sailors' mental health

The USS Abraham Lincoln, the US aircraft carrier that has spent months supporting American combat operations in the Middle East war against Iran, is set to return home, amid growing scrutiny over conditions faced by its roughly 5,000 sailors and Marines.Acting US navy secretary Hung Cao announced Friday (local time) that the carrier would return to the US as part of a planned rotation, saying the Lincoln's deployment had been extended because its mission demanded it. However, he downplayed the reports of the conditions and sailors.“The USS Abraham Lincoln crushed their deployment and will return home soon as part of a planned rotation,” Cao said in a statement. “Let me be clear: the safety and security of our Sailors and Marines always comes first.”The announcement comes amid reports of deteriorating conditions aboard the carrier, including intermittent food shortages, limited hygiene supplies, problems with toilets and water systems and a lack of regular port calls. Sailors and their families have also raised concerns about morale and mental health during the prolonged deployment.CNN reported that some sailors had described morale aboard the Lincoln as very low and said they had heard repeatedly about suicidal thoughts among fellow crew members.Two sailors assigned to the Lincoln strike group have also reportedly gone overboard in recent months and were rescued, while other sailors were reportedly stopped from jumping.“You used to be able to go to the ship store and get as many items as you want, with every hygiene product consistently available,” one sailor (talking anonymously) told CNN. Now there are limits on purchases and “hardly any hygiene products (are) readily available.”The Navy has disputed claims of a broader mental-health crisis aboard the carrier. “We have not observed an increase in suicidal ideations or attempts aboard the ship,” the Navy told CNN, adding that medical, religious and mental-health professionals were available to support service members.Cao also pushed back against reports portraying the sailors as victims, saying the media narrative had taken attention away from the mission and the threat facing US forces.He acknowledged that the deployment had placed sailors under significant strain, but said the carrier had continued to meet its operational demands.According to Cao, the Lincoln has spent 266 days deployed, including 200 days in a combat zone, while its strike group has conducted more than 10,000 sorties and dropped about 1.5 million pounds of ordnance He said the carrier's retention rates were among the highest in the Navy.Cao also acknowledged that some sailors had received mental-health treatment, although he said there had been no loss of life. He said meal plans had been adjusted when fresh supplies were unavailable, but “without a single meal being missed,” while calls home were sometimes restricted when the operational threat was too high.The Lincoln's prolonged deployment has also raised wider questions about the strain on the US Navy's carrier fleet. The Navy has traditionally planned around deployments of about seven months, but several carrier strike groups have exceeded that duration in recent years as US forces have responded to conflicts and security demands across multiple regions.The USS Gerald R Ford recently completed a 326-day deployment, the longest for a US aircraft carrier since the Vietnam War, while other carriers have also spent more than 250 days away from their home ports.Experts and former Navy officials have warned that repeated extensions can increase stress on sailors and their families, contribute to burnout and place additional strain on ships and equipment.The USS George Washington has been deployed to replace the Lincoln, which has been supporting US forces during the war against Iran. The Lincoln is carrying about 5,000 sailors and Marines.President Donald Trump has also dismissed concerns over the length of the carrier's deployment. Asked Friday whether it had gone on too long, Trump said, “No. Not nearly long enough.”Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth echoed that the conditions aboard the carrier have been “completely misrepresented.”Cao said the Lincoln's sailors had been pushed to their limits but had continued to carry out their mission.“They are rightly tired—but have never been out of the fight,” he said, calling the sailors and their families “the epitome of American strength and resilience.”
Article Summary: US aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln to return to US as part of planned rotation. Lincoln has spent 266 days deployed, including 200 days in a combat zone. Reports of food shortages, limited hygiene supplies, problems with toilets and water systems. Sailors and their families have also raised concerns about morale and mental health.

Article Title: Father of four Derrick Moore jumped into a Myrtle Beach rip current to save a 10-year-old girl; she survived, but he was swept away
Article Text:
According to a report by People, Derrick Moore, 47, of Loganville, Ga., helped the girl to safety at Myrtle Beach but was then pulled under.

Moored vanished after rescue effort

Family remembers father of four

Search joined by coast guard

Reportedly girl he saved is safe

A sad reminder of Rip currents

A South Carolina beach vacation turned tragic when a father of four died after swimming into a dangerous rip current to save a young girl. According to a report by People, Derrick Moore, 47, of Loganville, Ga. , helped the girl to safety at Myrtle Beach but was then pulled under. Moore’s family is mourning a man remembered as a devoted father, but details shared after his death shed light on the selfless act that preceded the tragedy.The report says that the Myrtle Beach Police Department and Myrtle Beach Fire Department responded around 8 p.m. Friday, Aug. 8 local time to reports of a missing swimmer near 10th Avenue South. Moore was pulled into the water after a young girl was caught in a rip current, according to authorities. He succeeded in saving the girl, but was then dragged down himself. Emergency workers started searching for Moore but couldn't find him that night. His body was discovered the next morning near 11th Avenue South in Myrtle Beach, authorities said.According to family members, Moore is a 47-year-old teacher and father of four from Loganville, Ga.His daughter described him as a loving father and his death has devastated the family. Moore was “loved deeply by those who knew him best,” his family said. According to reports, lifeguards were off duty when the incident occurred.Myrtle Beach police informed U.S. Coast Guard Sector Charleston watchstanders that a 47-year-old man had entered the water and not resurfaced, the Coast Guard said. The Coast Guard aided local agencies in the search and launched several assets, including a helicopter. Crews kept searching until the early hours of Saturday but could not find Moore. Police found his body Saturday morning near the shoreline in Myrtle Beach. Later the Coast Guard expressed its condolences to Moore’s family and friends who mourned his death.Moore apparently did not know the girl he went into the water to save. Authorities have not released the identity, whereabouts, or condition of the girl. But a man claiming to be the girl’s uncle later posted on social media that Moore had saved both him and his niece. The man allegedly responded to a social media post from one of Moore’s grieving sons, offering his condolences and saying he was trying to reach out to the family. Since then, social media users have reportedly tried to help connect the man with Moore’s relatives. No name has been released.For the uninitiated, rip currents are narrow, fast-moving channels of water that flow offshore. They can quickly sweep swimmers out to sea. They can be hard to find, especially if you are not used to the conditions on the ocean. Experts generally advise swimmers caught in a rip current not to directly fight the current by trying to swim straight back to shore. Instead, swimmers should try to remain calm and if needed float and swim parallel to the shore until out of the current before heading back to land. Moore's tragedy additionally emphasizes the dangers of entering the water to save another person. Someone caught in a rip current can panic and inadvertently put a rescuer in danger too. But for Moore’s family, his final moments are inseparable from the act of bravery that came before. He went into the water to help a child he didn’t know, getting her to safety before he himself was swept away.His passing leaves a community mourning a man known for putting another’s safety above his own, and four children without a father.Images Courtesy: istock and Facebook
Article Summary: Derrick Moore, 47, of Loganville, Ga., helped the girl to safety at Myrtle Beach. He succeeded in saving the girl, but was then dragged down himself. Emergency workers started searching for Moore but couldn't find him that night. His body was discovered the next morning near 11th Avenue South.

Article Title: Spanish explorers brought pigs to America for food in the 1500s; today, millions of feral swine roam at least 35 US states
Article Text:
Image AI generated

How Spanish explorers introduced pigs to the US in the 1500s

Image AI generated

How feral swine reproduce quickly and expand their populations

Which crops are most affected by feral swine

Why feral swine can be dangerous to people, pets, and livestock

When Spanish explorers brought pigs to what is now the southeastern United States in the 1500s, the animals were intended as a practical source of food rather than a threat to native ecosystems. Centuries of escapes, free-ranging livestock and later introductions of Eurasian wild boar changed that. According to the US Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, more than 6 million feral swine are estimated to occupy at least 35 US states. Their expansion has also been helped by people moving pigs into new areas, sometimes illegally, while their ability to breed quickly makes established populations difficult to contain. The animals now affect far more than farmland. They root through crops and pasture, damage fences and water systems, compete with native wildlife for food, disturb soil and habitat, and can carry dozens of diseases and parasites affecting livestock, pets, wildlife and people.The history of feral swine in the United States reaches back to the early period of European settlement. As per Mississippi State University, pigs were introduced into what is now the southeastern United States in the 1500s by Spanish explorer Hernando DeSoto.They were not originally brought over as an invasive species. Pigs were useful travelling animals because they could provide food during expeditions and settlement.That early introduction was followed by centuries in which pigs were allowed to roam freely, escaped from enclosures or established themselves outside human control. The population became more complicated in the early 1900s, when Eurasian wild boar were introduced into parts of the country for hunting. Where the two groups met, they interbred. Mississippi State University explains that many of the wild pigs seen today are therefore hybrids, descended from domestic pigs, Eurasian wild boar or both.The spread did not stop with accidental escapes. Human activity became an important part of the story. The illegal capture, transport and release of wild pigs has been a major reason populations have appeared far beyond their earlier range. According to the National Wildlife Federation, the popularity of feral hogs as an animal helped accelerate their spread into new parts of the country, particularly from the 1980s onwards.The scale of the population is striking. More than 6 million feral swine are now found across at least 35 states. The National Wildlife Federation similarly reported that the animals had reached at least 35 states and numbered more than 6 million, describing their expansion as the result of both natural movement and human transport.Their biology makes the expansion particularly difficult to reverse. Feral swine can begin reproducing at a young age, while females may produce large litters more than once a year. Females begin breeding at around eight months and produce two litters of four to 12 piglets every 12 to 15 months. That means even substantial losses within a population can be followed by rapid recovery when enough breeding animals remain.The animals are also highly adaptable. They are omnivores and can make use of crops, roots, insects, eggs, small animals and other available food. Feral hogs carry at least 30 viral and bacterial diseases and around 40 parasites, adding another layer to the problem as populations move through agricultural and natural landscapes.For farmers, the damage often begins below ground. Feral swine use their snouts to root through soil in search of food, disturbing newly planted fields and vegetation. They can trample crops, create wallows and damage fences, irrigation systems, water supplies and other farm infrastructure. Corn, rice, wheat, peanuts and other crops can be affected, while pastureland may be degraded by repeated feeding and soil disturbance.The consequences are not limited to the plants that pigs eat. Feral swine can transmit diseases to livestock, potentially leading to lower production, poorer reproductive outcomes, increased deaths and higher veterinary costs. They can also kill young livestock such as calves and lambs. The animals may contaminate or destroy livestock feed, turning a wildlife problem into a direct agricultural expense.Wildlife can be affected in less obvious ways. Feral swine compete with native animals for food such as acorns and other forest nuts, while also eating insects, amphibians, reptiles, eggs and small mammals. Their rooting can remove vegetation and disturb soil, leaving areas more vulnerable to erosion and invasive plants. APHIS has linked feral swine to declines among nearly 300 native plant and animal species, including species already facing conservation pressures.Feral swine are not confined to remote woodland. They can move through farmland, parks, suburban areas and other places where people live or work. Animals entering roads and airports can create collision risks, while pigs accustomed to receiving food from people may become less wary and more aggressive. Dogs and other pets can also be attacked.There are public health concerns alongside those physical risks. Feral swine can carry at least 30 diseases and nearly 40 types of parasites capable of affecting people, livestock, pets and wildlife. Some infections can pass through contaminated food, while pigs can also contribute to bacterial contamination of water in areas where they are active. Diseases identified in the material include E. coli, toxoplasmosis and trichinosis. Pseudorabies is another concern, particularly because it can be fatal to cats and dogs exposed through contact with infected feral swine carcasses.The damage can also reach places that are not normally thought of as wildlife habitat. Feral swine can root through lawns, golf courses, parks, cemeteries and recreational grounds, while their digging and wallowing can damage archaeological sites, historic locations and culturally significant areas. The animals’ expansion has been driven not only by their ability to survive in the wild but by people moving them, deliberately or accidentally, into new areas.The result is an unusual case of an animal introduced for a practical purpose centuries ago becoming a nationwide management challenge. The pigs that travelled with European settlers were not destined to become an invasive population. But escapes, free-ranging livestock, later hunting introductions, interbreeding and illegal relocation gradually changed that history. With millions of feral swine now spread across the US, the original introduction in the 1500s has left a legacy that is still expanding.
Article Summary: More than 6 million feral swine are estimated to occupy at least 35 US states. They root through crops and pasture, damage fences and water systems, compete with native wildlife for food, disturb soil and habitat, and can carry dozens of diseases and parasites. Feral swine can transmit diseases to livestock, potentially leading to lower production and poorer reproductive outcomes.

Article Title: '30 civilans killed': Baloch activist shares video of 'Pakistani war crime', seeks US intervention
Article Text:
Mir Yar Baloch has urged the US administration to impose sanctions on Pakistan.

Baloch leader seeks US sanctions

Pakistan disputes airstrike allegations

Protests erupt over reported civilian deaths

Mir Yar Baloch, a Baloch leader, has accused Pakistan 's military of carrying out an airstrike in Balochistan that allegedly killed 30 civilians, including women, children and infants.He claimed that video footage from the August 12 attack in Surab's Gidar Goandhan area provides evidence of the military operation and said he plans to take the matter to the International Criminal Court."The Republic of Balochistan has obtained video footage of the Surab Air Strike conducted by the external terrorist forces of Pakistan on 12th August, which killed 30 innocent Balochistan civilians including women, children, and infants and injured dozens more. The missile debris clearly visible in the video constitute irrefutable proof of Pakistan's terrorism. They also thoroughly expose Pakistan's military spokesperson, DG ISPR, who deliberately misled the global community on national media by claiming the attack was merely an IED blast on the ground," Mir Yar Baloch wrote on X.Mir Yar Baloch has urged the US administration to impose sanctions on Pakistan and halt military support, including F-16 engine spare parts and upgrades to fighter jets and missile programmes."The Republic of Balochistan urges the Trump administration to impose strict economic sanctions on Pakistan, cancel the delivery of spare parts for F-16 engines, and halt all upgradation package to its fighter jets and missile program.The Pakistan military and air force are massively employing these very weapons and aircraft against the people of the independent Republic of Balochistan. Washington must hold Pakistan fully accountable for its war crimes in Balochistan," he added.The two sides have given sharply different accounts of what happened in Surab, leaving the circumstances of the incident and the actual civilian death toll disputed.Pakistan's military has rejected the claim of an airstrike and said the casualties were caused by a premature explosion involving a vehicle-borne improvised explosive device allegedly being assembled by militants.The Inter-Services Public Relations said the initial blast killed eight militants and that a secondary explosion involving other explosives stored at the site also caused civilian deaths."However, the blast and secondary detonation of other explosives stored there by the terrorists of Indian Proxy have also reportedly caused tragic casualties of three nearby civilians," the ISPR said.The military said Pakistani forces and Balochistan Police subsequently killed 10 more individuals, taking the reported militant death toll to 18. Two Pakistani soldiers were also injured during the exchange of fire.The competing accounts have come amid protests in Balochistan following reports of civilian deaths in the Surab area.The Balochistan Post reported that more than 20 people were initially killed and at least 16 injured in the incident. Some local residents, however, claimed that the actual death toll could be higher.
Article Summary: Baloch leader Mir Yar Baloch has accused Pakistan's military of carrying out an airstrike in Balochistan that allegedly killed 30 civilians. Article Title: 'Water is our red line': Shehbaz Sharif threatens India with 'direct response' over Indus Treaty
Article Text:
Shehbaz Sharif speaking on eve of Pakistan's Independence Day

Pakistan has yet again raked up India’s suspension of the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT), with its Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif threatening a “direct response” to New Delhi’s move, which came days after the Pahalgam terror attack in Jammu and Kashmir in April last year."The Prime Minister said that India has proven itself an enemy of peace by unilaterally and illegally suspending the Indus Waters Treaty. He announced that every drop of Pakistan's water is our red line. There will be no compromise on the water issue. If India does not come to the right path, we will give it a direct response," the Pakistan Prime Minister's Office said in a statement on X.Sharif, speaking at an event on the eve of Pakistan’s Independence Day (August 14), sought to portray India as an “enemy of peace” over New Delhi’s decision to keep the IWT in abeyance following the April 22 Pahalgam terror attack, in which 26 civilians were killed.He said New Delhi had proved itself an “enemy” of peace by putting the treaty in abeyance."India proved itself an enemy of peace by unilaterally and illegally suspending the Indus Waters Treaty. I declare in clear terms that every single drop of Pakistan's water is our red line. Article Summary: Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif threatens a "direct response" to India's suspension of the Indus Waters Treaty. Article Title: Why US is questioning Pakistan's Rs 3 trillion defence spending
Article Text:
The US also criticised Islamabad for not publishing its executive budget proposal within a reasonable period (representative image)

US asks Pakistan to improve defence and debt transparency

Pakistan's defence allocation rises to Rs 3 trillion

Defence spending remains a key transparency concern

The US state department has flagged a lack of adequate parliamentary and civilian oversight of Pakistan's military and intelligence spending, while also raising concerns over limited disclosure of government debt and delays in publishing the executive budget proposal.The concerns were highlighted in the 2026 Fiscal Transparency Report, which assessed Pakistan's public financial transparency and identified gaps in the country's budgetary and fiscal disclosure practices.The report noted that Pakistan made its enacted budget and end-of-year financial statements widely available online. However, it said military and intelligence budgets remained outside adequate parliamentary or civilian public scrutiny.“The military and intelligence budgets were not subject to adequate parliamentary or civilian public oversight,” the report said.The US also criticised Islamabad for not publishing its executive budget proposal within a reasonable period.According to the assessment, this limits the time available for lawmakers and civil society to examine government spending before the budget is adopted.The state department called for three key changes to Pakistan's fiscal transparency framework.It urged Islamabad to make its executive budget proposal publicly available within a reasonable period, disclose detailed information about government debt obligations, including liabilities linked to state-owned enterprises, and bring military and intelligence agency budgets under parliamentary or civilian public oversight.The report also raised concerns about Pakistan's disclosure of public debt, saying only limited information was available on debt obligations, including those of major state-owned enterprises.At the same time, the US assessment acknowledged some positive aspects of Pakistan's public financial system.It said the country's supreme audit institution met international standards of independence and noted that its audit reports were published in a timely manner and contained substantive findings.The US assessment comes against the backdrop of a substantial increase in Pakistan's defence allocation for the 2026-27 financial year.In June, Pakistan's federal government proposed allocating Rs 3 trillion for defence services, up 17.65 per cent from the previous year's initial allocation of Rs 2.55 trillion, according to Dawn.The proposed defence services allocation amounts to about 2.08 per cent of Pakistan's projected GDP of Rs 143.6 trillion and nearly 16 per cent of the federal government's total outlay of Rs 18.77 trillion.Spending on civil works related to military infrastructure was projected to rise 7.92 per cent to Rs 363.16 billion, from Rs 336.49 billion previously.Military pensions are accounted for separately from the main defence services budget. The government has allocated Rs 822 billion for retired military personnel under the federal pension outlay, according to Dawn.The allocation for defence administration was set at Rs 10.9 billion, compared with Rs 7.9 billion in the outgoing fiscal year's original budget. That allocation was later revised to Rs 11.75 billion.Major military imports and defence acquisitions are generally funded outside the main defence services allocation and remain undisclosed.The US state department's assessment therefore highlights a distinction between Pakistan's publicly disclosed defence allocation and the wider military spending that may not be fully visible through the country's budgetary documents.The state department's recommendations focus on bringing military and intelligence expenditure into the broader framework of public financial oversight.While the report recognised that Pakistan publishes key budget documents, it identified defence and intelligence spending, debt disclosure and the timing of budget publication as areas requiring greater transparency.The recommendations would require Pakistan to give lawmakers and the public greater visibility into military and intelligence allocations, as well as government liabilities linked to state-owned enterprises.
Article Summary: US asks Pakistan to improve defence and debt transparency. Pakistan's defence allocation rises to Rs 3 trillion for 2026-27 financial year. US state department flagged a lack of adequate parliamentary and civilian oversight of Pakistan's military and intelligence spending. Report also raised concerns over limited disclosure of government debt and delays in publishing executive budget proposal.

Article Title: PML-N set to form 'government' in PoK after two former 'premiers' lose strongholds in third phase
Article Text:
Two former PoK premiers lost their strongholds in the third phase of elections marred by violence and rigging allegations, as the PML-N emerged dominant

Two former so-called prime ministers of Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) lost their traditional strongholds in the third phase of elections, according to unofficial results released on Tuesday, while incumbent premier Faisal Mumtaz Rathore of the Pakistan People's Party (PPP) retained his seat.The latest results came after voting in four constituencies on Monday, with the election process again overshadowed by violence and allegations of rigging. Polling in the remaining seven constituencies was postponed over concerns about the law-and-order situation and is expected to be held on August 21, according to the region's election commission.The PPP won two of the four seats contested in the third phase, while the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) and the Awami Dast-o-Bazu Party won one each. The latter is backed by both Jamaat-e-Islami and Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI).Former prime minister and Muslim Conference president Sardar Attique Ahmed Khan, who was backed by the PML-N, lost the seat in Western Bagh's Dhirkot constituency to Awami Dast-o-Bazu Party candidate Sardar Sajid Iqbal, according to unofficial results. The seat had been held by the Muslim Conference/PML-N since 1985.In Central Bagh, PPP's Zia Qamar retained the seat, defeating PML-N candidate Mushtaq Minhas.Former premier Sardar Tanveer Ilyas, who joined the Istehkam-i-Pakistan Party, secured only a few thousand votes.The result in Eastern Bagh remained pending after authorities ordered a re-poll at 12 polling stations. PML-N candidate Sardar Mir Akbar was leading based on results from 174 of the constituency's 186 polling stations, followed by PPP candidate Sardar Qamaruz Zaman Khan.The election comes against the backdrop of a striking shift in the Pakistani government's treatment of the protest movement that has rocked PoK for months.Just days before the final phase of voting, Pakistan's defence minister Khawaja Asif had described the protesters as "enemies of Pakistan" and ruled out talks with them. But Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif's adviser Rana Sanaullah subsequently said 99% of those associated with the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) were "patriotic brothers", promising that a PML-N government would engage with the group and seek to resolve its demands.The reversal in rhetoric came as the PML-N emerged as the dominant force in the election and prepared to form the next government in the region. The party has secured 25 of the 45 directly elected seats so far, while the PPP has won 12 and the Awami Dast-o-Bazu Party one.The first two phases, held on July 27 and August 2, were also marked by violent protests and allegations of widespread rigging, with the PML-N and PPP accusing each other of electoral malpractice. Supporters of the two parties clashed at several polling stations.The JAAC has been protesting across the region since early June, with demands including the abolition of 12 refugee seats that it says can be used to influence the formation of governments in PoK.The group has alleged that more than 40 people were killed during violence surrounding the first phase of voting and that around 400 protesters had been killed since the protests began. The Pakistani government has rejected the higher figure as exaggerated, while Sanaullah has acknowledged that deaths from the unrest were in the "double figures".India does not recognise Pakistan's control over the territory, maintaining that Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh are integral and inalienable parts of India and describing Pakistan's presence in areas under its control as "illegal and forcible occupation".
Article Summary: Two former so-called prime ministers of Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) lost their traditional strongholds in the third phase of elections. Incumbent premier Faisal Mumtaz Rathore of the Pakistan People's Party (PPP) retained his seat. Polling in the remaining seven constituencies was postponed over concerns about the law-and-order situation.
